changes.before: "explain": "MRI is the reference standard for the radiographically occult hip fracture. It shows the low-signal line on T1 and the surrounding oedema on a fluid-sensitive sequence from the day of injury, and a limited two-sequence coronal protocol takes only a few minutes. CT misses a proportion of undisplaced femoral neck fractures, particularly in osteoporotic bone where the trabecular detail it depends on has already been lost, so a negative CT does not exclude the diagnosis \u2014 though CT is the reasonable substitute where MRI is contraindicated or unavailable. Scintigraphy needs a day or more in an elderly patient before it becomes reliable. Waiting ten days is the worst option of the four: it leaves an undisplaced intracapsular fracture to displace in a patient who is immobile in the meantime, and displacement is what converts a fixable fracture into an arthroplasty.",

changes.before: "explain": "Four features move together here. The distribution is bilateral, symmetric and proximal \u2014 metacarpophalangeal joints, proximal interphalangeal joints and wrists \u2014 with the distal interphalangeal joints spared, which is close to the opposite of psoriatic disease. The density is reduced periarticularly, because hyperaemic synovitis resorbs the adjacent trabecular bone. The erosions sit at the margin, at the bare area between the edge of the articular cartilage and the capsular insertion, where synovium lies against unprotected bone. And there is no new bone at all, which is what separates rheumatoid arthritis from every spondyloarthritis. The action matters as much as the label: a visible radiographic erosion is already a late finding, so ultrasound or MRI, which show synovitis and bone marrow oedema before the cortex is breached, is what changes treatment inside the window in which treatment works best.",

changes.before: "explain": "Synovitis comes first and shows as fusiform periarticular soft-tissue swelling; the hyperaemia that accompanies it resorbs trabecular bone next to the joint, giving periarticular osteopenia. Pannus then reaches the bare area at the joint margin, where no cartilage protects the bone, and erodes it. Only after that does the pannus thin the cartilage across the whole joint, which is why the narrowing of rheumatoid arthritis is uniform rather than confined to a loaded compartment as in osteoarthritis. Deformity, subluxation and finally bony ankylosis \u2014 commonest in the carpus \u2014 end the sequence. The order is the argument for imaging early with a modality that sees synovium: by the time the radiograph shows the third step, the damage that treatment was meant to prevent has happened.",

changes.before: "explain": "Three millimetres is the upper limit of the anterior atlanto-dental interval in an adult; up to five is accepted in a child, whose ligaments are laxer and whose odontoid is incompletely ossified. Beyond the adult limit the transverse ligament has been destroyed by pannus and the atlas slides forward on the axis in flexion, which is precisely what happens when an anaesthetist positions a head for laryngoscopy. The interval that predicts neurological injury, though, is the one behind the peg \u2014 the space left for the cord between the odontoid and the posterior arch \u2014 because as the anterior gap opens, that posterior space closes. Radiographs answer the question of movement; MRI is what shows pannus, cord compression and cord signal change, and vertical migration of the peg through the foramen magnum is the more dangerous and easily missed second pattern.",

changes.before: "answer": "Erosive osteoarthritis erodes centrally. The subchondral plate collapses in the middle of the joint while osteophytes hold up the margins, producing the gull-wing outline on the frontal view, and sometimes a saw-tooth appearance where the opposing surface is remodelled. It sits in a hand that shows osteoarthritis elsewhere \u2014 first carpometacarpal and proximal interphalangeal involvement, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and subchondral cysts \u2014 with normal bone density and no periosteal reaction. Psoriatic arthritis erodes at the margins, where the bare area lies, and then lays down new bone: ill-defined fluffy periosteal reaction along the shaft next to the erosion, ossification at entheses, and in advanced disease pencil-in-cup deformity and acro-osteolysis of the tuft. Its distribution is asymmetric and follows a whole ray rather than a row of equivalent joints, the soft tissues may show a uniformly swollen digit rather than a joint-centred swelling, and bone density is preserved. Neither shows the periarticular osteopenia of rheumatoid arthritis, and neither spares new bone the way rheumatoid arthritis does.",

changes.before: "explain": "The two questions that settle almost every eroding hand are where in the joint the erosion sits and whether the bone is reacting. Central erosion with marginal osteophytes is a degenerative process eating through a thinned subchondral plate; marginal erosion with adjacent proliferation is an enthesis-driven inflammatory one. Distribution is the cross-check: osteoarthritis, erosive or not, picks out the same joints on both hands in a recognisable pattern, whereas psoriatic disease is asymmetric and runs down a ray. Where the film is genuinely equivocal, the clinical examination \u2014 nail pitting and onycholysis, a scalp or natal cleft plaque, dactylitis, enthesitis at the heel \u2014 usually decides it faster than more imaging will.",

changes.before: "explain": "Calcium pyrophosphate crystals deposit in fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage, and the triangular fibrocartilage is one of the four places worth looking for them, with the knee menisci, the symphysis pubis and the acetabular labrum. Their arthropathy is degenerative in character \u2014 narrowing, sclerosis and prominent subchondral cysts \u2014 but it appears in joints that primary osteoarthritis has little reason to visit, and the radiocarpal joint is the classic one: crystal-driven failure of the scapholunate ligament lets the interval widen and the capitate migrate proximally between scaphoid and lunate. Rheumatoid disease also destroys the carpus, but with periarticular osteopenia, marginal erosions and erosion of the ulnar styloid rather than chondrocalcinosis. Haemochromatosis is the important companion diagnosis and produces chondrocalcinosis too, but its signature is hook-like osteophytes on the radial aspect of the second and third metacarpal heads, and those joints are stated to be normal here.",

changes.before: "explain": "Gout is the arthritis that breaks the usual coupling between erosion and joint destruction, and that dissociation \u2014 substantial erosion with a joint space that still looks reasonable and bone that is still dense \u2014 is what should bring it to mind on any hand or foot film. The distribution helps: the first metatarsophalangeal joint, the midfoot, the olecranon bursa, the knee and the hands in longstanding disease, characteristically asymmetric. Two cautions on confirmation: the double contour sign and dual-energy CT are much less sensitive in the first attack than in established disease, so a negative study does not exclude gout in an acute joint, and an eroded joint with a soft-tissue mass that turns out to have no urate needs a different explanation, including infection.",

changes.before: "explain": "Where the ossification runs tells you which structure is ossifying. In ankylosing spondylitis it is the outer fibres of the annulus fibrosus, which run vertically from one vertebral corner to the next, so the syndesmophyte is thin, vertical and marginal, and the disease is symmetric \u2014 including its sacroiliitis, which is bilateral and equal. In psoriatic and reactive arthritis the ossification forms in the paravertebral tissues away from the disc margin, so it is bulky, coarse, asymmetric and often skips levels, matching an asymmetric or unilateral sacroiliitis. Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis is the third pattern and the one most often confused with the second: flowing ossification along the anterior longitudinal ligament across four or more contiguous vertebrae, with the disc heights preserved and the sacroiliac joints and facet joints uninvolved, which is why the sacroiliitis described here excludes it.",

changes.before: "explain": "The tempo is the diagnosis. Bacterial enzymes and the host response destroy cartilage over days, so the whole joint space disappears at once and both articular surfaces erode, with no time for the new bone that any chronic arthropathy would have produced. Nothing else on the list moves that fast: rheumatoid arthritis does not destroy a knee in three weeks and is rarely monoarticular at onset, rapidly progressive osteoarthritis is a real but slower entity and a diagnosis of exclusion, and a neuropathic joint shows the triad of increased density, debris and dislocation with abundant fragmentation, in a patient whose pain is characteristically less than the film suggests. changes.before: "explain": "Probably benign means a likelihood of malignancy greater than zero but no more than two per cent \u2014 low enough that surveillance is safer than biopsying every such lesion, but not low enough to ignore. The obligation the category carries is a protocol, not a vague plan: a unilateral study at six months, then bilateral at twelve and twenty-four months, and stability across two to three years permits a downgrade to benign. Three constraints go with it. The category should be assigned after a complete diagnostic workup rather than from a screening study, it is not appropriate for a palpable finding or where the patient cannot or will not comply with follow-up, and the findings for which the evidence supports it are few: a solitary circumscribed non-calcified mass, a focal asymmetry that effaces on spot compression, and a group of round or punctate calcifications. A finding that enlarges or changes during surveillance is biopsied.",

changes.before: "explain": "Rotating the tube from the oblique to a true lateral swings the lateral part of the breast downwards and the medial part upwards, so a lateral lesion drops and a medial lesion rises \u2014 the aide-memoire is that lead sinks and muffins rise. Watching the lesion move in the predicted direction is how you prove that the two views show the same object rather than two different ones, which is the whole point of triangulation and the reason a mass seen on one view alone gets a second projection before anything else. The true lateral also supplies the vertical coordinate a biopsy or wire localisation needs, and it is the projection on which milk of calcium layers into teacup shapes that the craniocaudal view shows only as smudges.",

changes.before: "explain": "Radiological-pathological concordance is the last step of every image-guided biopsy and the one that catches the sampling error. A finding carrying at least a ninety-five per cent likelihood of malignancy cannot be explained by fibrocystic change, so the benign result is discordant whether or not the pathologist is confident about what is on the slide, and the pathway is repeat sampling or, more usually at this level of suspicion, surgical excision. Accepting it and returning the patient to screening is the failure mode this check exists to prevent. Repeating the biopsy stereotactically is the wrong technique for a mass that ultrasound can see, and short-interval mammography leaves a probable cancer in place. The same discipline governs the lesions that are excised despite a benign core result because of their upgrade rate at excision \u2014 atypical ductal hyperplasia, a radial scar or complex sclerosing lesion, papillary lesions, and a discordant result of any kind.",

changes.before: "explain": "Each category is a probability band, and each band names an action. Category 1 and category 2 both carry an essentially zero likelihood and both mean routine screening; category 2 differs only in that a benign finding has been described. Category 3 is above zero but no more than two per cent and means short-interval surveillance. The three category 4 subdivisions run above two to ten, above ten to fifty, and above fifty to below ninety-five per cent, and all three mean tissue diagnosis \u2014 the subdivision guides how the result is then handled rather than whether to biopsy. Category 5 is ninety-five per cent or more. Two categories deliberately sit outside this ladder: category 0 is not a suspicion level at all but a statement that the workup is incomplete, and category 6 is a cancer already proved by biopsy.",

changes.before: "explain": "Four things identify a scar: it is at the operative site, marked by clips; it changes shape markedly between the two projections, because it is a plane of fibrosis rather than a mass; it has no central density; and above all it becomes less conspicuous or stays stable over successive studies, since scar tissue and post-radiotherapy oedema regress. Recurrence does the opposite \u2014 a scar that becomes denser, develops a central mass, or acquires new calcifications is the finding that triggers biopsy. MRI is genuinely useful where the mammogram is equivocal, because mature scar beyond about a year typically enhances little while recurrence enhances, but ordering it against a four-year stable appearance buys false positives rather than information. Comparison with the previous films is the whole of the argument here, which is why the prior studies are part of the examination and not an optional extra.",

changes.before: "answer": "In the first case MRI earns its place. Lobular carcinoma grows in single-file strands without forming a discrete mass or a desmoplastic reaction, so it is the type that mammography most often misses or underestimates, particularly in dense tissue; MRI has the highest sensitivity of any breast technique for invasive disease and is used here to measure the extent of the tumour, to look for multifocal or multicentric disease and for a contralateral cancer that would change the operation. The condition attached is that MRI also finds lesions that prove benign, so any additional finding that would alter surgery is biopsied first, usually under ultrasound after a targeted second-look scan, rather than acted on directly. In the second case supplemental MRI is offered to women at high lifetime risk \u2014 carriers of a pathogenic BRCA1, BRCA2 or comparable variant and their untested first-degree relatives, women whose family history puts their lifetime risk above roughly a fifth on a model that accounts for it, and women irradiated to the chest in adolescence or early adulthood \u2014 but it is an addition to mammography rather than a replacement, because MRI is poor at showing calcifications, which is how a large share of ductal carcinoma in situ presents. Current ACR guidance does not require routine menstrual-cycle scheduling; repeat imaging for a genuinely limited examination is individualised.",

Current ACR guidance does not require routine menstrual-cycle scheduling; repeat imaging for a genuinely limited examination is individualised.",

changes.before: "explain": "Fibroglandular tissue attenuates x-rays much as a tumour does, so a cancer surrounded by it has little contrast against its background and mammographic sensitivity falls with increasing density \u2014 the masking effect that produced this interval cancer. Separately and independently, high breast density is itself a risk factor for developing breast cancer, so the two effects compound rather than offset. That is the argument for supplemental imaging in dense breasts: tomosynthesis raises cancer detection and lowers recall by separating overlapping tissue, and supplemental ultrasound, contrast-enhanced mammography and MRI each find additional cancers, with MRI shown to reduce the interval cancer rate in extremely dense breasts. The honest caveat is that a mortality benefit from supplemental screening has not been demonstrated, and every additional test brings false positives with it. Density is a qualitative judgement made on the current study and can change over time, with hormonal status and with weight.",

changes.before: "explain": "Lung volume is the discriminator that does most of the work on a neonatal chest film, because it follows directly from where the abnormality sits. Fluid in the interstitium leaves the air spaces open and the lungs large; absent surfactant collapses the air spaces and makes the lungs small. Everything else \u2014 gestation, mode of delivery, the tempo over the following two days, and the response to surfactant \u2014 is confirmatory. The pair also illustrates why the neonatal film is read alongside the gestational age and the clinical course rather than in isolation: the same granular pattern in a term infant should raise pneumonia, and coarse patchy shadowing with hyperinflation in a term or post-term infant with a history of stained liquor points instead to meconium aspiration.",
changes.after: "explain": "Lung volume is the discriminator that does most of the work on a neonatal chest film, because it follows directly from where the abnormality sits. Fluid in the interstitium leaves the air spaces open and the lungs large; absent surfactant collapses the air spaces and makes the lungs small. Everything else — gestation, mode of delivery, the tempo over the following two days, and the response to surfactant — is confirmatory. changes.before: "explain": "The course identifies the vessel before the tip is judged. The umbilical artery runs caudally to the internal iliac artery before turning up the aorta, so an initial dip into the pelvis is the signature of an arterial catheter; the umbilical vein runs straight up through the falciform ligament and the left portal vein into the ductus venosus, so a catheter that only ascends is venous. Acceptable arterial tip positions are high, between the sixth and ninth thoracic vertebrae \u2014 above the coeliac axis and below the ductus arteriosus \u2014 or low, between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae, below the renal arteries; the intervening stretch is avoided because it lies across the origins of the visceral vessels. The venous tip should sit at the junction of the inferior vena cava and the right atrium, around the eighth or ninth thoracic level. The two failures worth knowing are a venous tip that stops short in the liver, which risks portal vein thrombosis and extravasation of hypertonic infusate into the parenchyma, and a tip advanced into the right atrium, which risks arrhythmia, thrombus and pericardial tamponade.",

Acceptable arterial tip positions are high, between the sixth and ninth thoracic vertebrae — above the coeliac axis and below the ductus arteriosus — or low, between the third and fourth lumbar vertebrae, below the renal arteries; the intervening stretch is avoided because it lies across the origins of the visceral vessels. changes.before: "explain": "Dilated, separated loops with a loss of the normal polygonal gas pattern are the earliest and least specific finding, and by themselves they support only a suspicion. Intramural gas \u2014 a bubbly or curvilinear lucency within the bowel wall, produced by gas-forming organisms in a damaged mucosa \u2014 is the finding that establishes the diagnosis. Branching lucencies over the liver are that gas carried back in the portal venous system, and they mark more extensive disease and a worse prognosis. Free intraperitoneal gas means the bowel has perforated and is the one finding that is an absolute indication for surgery; it appears as gas outlining the falciform ligament on the supine film, as both sides of the bowel wall becoming visible, or as a lucency over the liver on a left lateral decubitus view, which is the projection to request in an infant too unwell to be sat up. A loop that stays in the same position and the same shape across serial films is a further sign of a segment that is no longer viable, and ultrasound adds bowel wall thickness, perfusion and free fluid that the radiograph cannot show.",

changes.before: "explain": "Bile-stained vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proved otherwise, and the whole pathway is built around how quickly the midgut dies once its vascular pedicle twists. Resuscitation and a nasogastric tube come first, both to decompress the stomach and to confirm the character of the aspirate. The plain film is quick and can show a double bubble, a gasless abdomen or dilated loops \u2014 but it is very often normal, so it can raise the suspicion and cannot lower it. The upper gastrointestinal contrast study is the reference standard: it shows where the duodenojejunal flexure lies, which should be to the left of the left-sided pedicle at the level of the duodenal bulb, and in volvulus it shows a corkscrew or beaked duodenum. A twisted midgut then goes straight to a Ladd procedure. Ultrasound showing the superior mesenteric vein lying anterior or to the left of the artery, or a whirlpool of vessels wrapping the pedicle, is increasingly used and can make the diagnosis quickly, but in most units a normal ultrasound does not by itself exclude malrotation.",

A twisted midgut then goes straight to a Ladd procedure. Ultrasound showing the superior mesenteric vein lying anterior or to the left of the artery, or a whirlpool of vessels wrapping the pedicle, is increasingly used and can make the diagnosis quickly, but in most units a normal ultrasound does not by itself exclude malrotation.",

changes.before: "explain": "The two bubbles are the distended stomach and the dilated duodenal cap proximal to the obstruction, and what discriminates among the causes is whether any gas has passed beyond them. Complete absence of distal gas means a complete obstruction, and in a neonate with trisomy 21 that is duodenal atresia, which needs no contrast study before surgery. Gas beyond the second bubble means the obstruction is incomplete \u2014 a fenestrated web, an annular pancreas, or malrotation with Ladd bands \u2014 and those do need a contrast study, both to define the anatomy and because malrotation carries the risk of volvulus. The trap to hold on to is the converse: a neonate vomiting bile whose film is normal or near-normal still needs an urgent upper gastrointestinal study, because a midgut volvulus can produce very little to see on a plain film and is the one diagnosis here that cannot wait.",

The trap to hold on to is the converse: a neonate vomiting bile whose film is normal or near-normal still needs an urgent upper gastrointestinal study, because a midgut volvulus can produce very little to see on a plain film and is the one diagnosis here that cannot wait.",

changes.before: "explain": "Ileocolic intussusception at this age is usually idiopathic, following lymphoid hypertrophy after a viral illness, and ultrasound is both sensitive and specific enough to be the diagnostic test \u2014 the target on the transverse image and the pseudo-kidney on the longitudinal one. Reduction by air, or by fluid under ultrasound guidance, is the treatment, and it succeeds in the large majority. It is done with a surgeon informed and theatre available, because of the small risk of perforation during the procedure and because a failed reduction goes on to operation. The contraindications are perforation, peritonitis and shock, none of which is present here. CT adds radiation to a child and delays a treatment that is already available; a lead point such as a Meckel diverticulum, a duplication cyst, lymphoma or the bowel wall haematoma of Henoch-Schoenlein purpura is looked for in children outside the typical age range or after repeated recurrence. A short small-bowel-only intussusception found incidentally is usually transient and needs no intervention.",

changes.before: "explain": "Both halves of the answer matter. The modality is wrong because the femoral head is entirely cartilaginous until around four to six months, so a neonatal radiograph shows an empty acetabulum and unreliable landmarks, while ultrasound images the cartilaginous head and the acetabular roof directly and adds a dynamic assessment of stability under stress. The timing is wrong because physiological ligamentous laxity in the first weeks of life produces immature-looking hips that resolve spontaneously, so scanning too early converts normal newborns into patients; a scan at around six weeks is the compromise that finds the hips that need treating without treating the ones that do not. This applies to screening on the basis of a risk factor \u2014 breech presentation, a first-degree family history, oligohydramnios \u2014 in an infant whose examination is normal. An infant with a positive Ortolani or Barlow test is imaged and referred to orthopaedics sooner, and a frankly dislocated irreducible hip is discussed immediately.",

changes.before: "explain": "In a normal neonate the rectum is the widest part of the large bowel, so a rectum narrower than the sigmoid \u2014 a rectosigmoid index below one \u2014 is abnormal in itself, and a transition in calibre above it marks the boundary between the aganglionic distal segment, which cannot relax, and the dilated ganglionic bowel proximal to it. Suction rectal biopsy is what confirms the diagnosis; the enema shows where to expect the transition and how much bowel is involved. Two technical points determine whether the study works: it is done without a preceding rectal examination or washout, either of which can decompress the transition zone and hide it, and delayed films are taken, since retention of contrast beyond 24 hours supports the diagnosis. The alternatives differ in the calibre of the colon along its whole length: meconium ileus gives a microcolon with filling defects in the terminal ileum and points to cystic fibrosis, ileal atresia gives an unused microcolon with no pellets, and small left colon syndrome shows an abrupt calibre change at the splenic flexure in an infant of a diabetic mother and resolves without surgery.",

changes.before: "explain": "The single most useful question in this area is whether the injury fits what the child is physically capable of doing. Fractures in non-ambulant infants are uncommon and are the group in which inflicted injury is most frequent, which is why the developmental history is recorded before the film is reported. The survey is a protocol rather than an ad hoc set of films because its purpose is to find fractures that are clinically silent, and the follow-up survey exists because callus makes visible what the acute study could not \u2014 particularly rib and metaphyseal injuries. The last sentence is the one that is easiest to get wrong in either direction: imaging can describe the injuries and their probable ages and mechanisms, and it can say whether the account offered fits, but the determination is made by the safeguarding process rather than by the radiologist alone.",

changes.before: "explain": "Three features identify the appendix and all three are needed: it ends blindly, it does not peristalse, and it arises from the caecal pole where the taeniae converge. A tube that peristalses is small bowel, and calling it a normal appendix is how a false negative is manufactured. Graded compression is the technique that makes the search possible \u2014 steady, increasing pressure with the linear probe displaces gas-filled bowel out of the field and brings the appendix closer, which both improves resolution and tests compressibility. The inflamed appendix is non-compressible, aperistaltic, over 6 mm outer-to-outer, often with an echogenic hyperaemic halo of inflamed fat around it. A perforated appendix may indeed decompress, but it does not acquire peristalsis. Nodes are ovoid with an echogenic hilum, not tubular in continuity along their length.",

changes.before: "explain": "2.1 plus 4.6 plus 2.1 gives 8.8 mm. The measurement that matters is outer wall to outer wall in a true transverse section, not the lumen and not an oblique cut through a curving appendix, both of which mislead. The conventional upper limit of normal is 6 mm, but the threshold behaves poorly on its own: a normal appendix can distend to 7 mm with gas or faecal material, and diameters between 6 and 8 mm are a genuine grey zone in which secondary signs decide \u2014 non-compressibility, mural hyperaemia on colour Doppler, an appendicolith, echogenic inflamed periappendiceal fat, and focal tenderness under the probe. At 8.8 mm with non-compressibility the diagnosis is secure. Beware the opposite error too: pressing too hard flattens the measurement and can talk you out of a real appendicitis.",

changes.before: "explain": "A non-visualised appendix is a common and honest result, and the report must say plainly that it is not a negative study. The causes are worth knowing because several are correctable: a retrocaecal or deep pelvic position, overlying gas, obesity, guarding that defeats compression, a perforated appendix that has decompressed, and inexperience with the technique. What softens the result is the complete absence of secondary signs \u2014 no free fluid, no echogenic fat, no nodes, no tenderness under the probe \u2014 which lowers the probability but never to zero. The next step depends on the patient in front of you: CT in a non-pregnant adult whose pain persists or whose inflammatory markers are rising, MRI in pregnancy, and structured clinical reassessment where the story is settling. What is not acceptable is a conclusion that reads as though appendicitis has been excluded.",

changes.before: "explain": "Two nodes \u2014 those of 6 mm and 8 mm \u2014 meet a 5 mm short-axis threshold. A commonly used working definition of mesenteric adenitis asks for three or more right iliac fossa nodes of at least 5 mm in short axis together with a normal appendix, sometimes with mild ileal or caecal wall thickening, so on this study the label is not fully earned even though the picture fits. That nuance matters less than the discipline behind it: nodes are non-specific, they are common in children and they are frequently present in appendicitis itself, so enlarged nodes never exclude an inflamed appendix. The finding that carries the weight here is the appendix \u2014 compressible, 4 mm, blind-ending \u2014 which is a genuinely normal appendix. Always measure nodes in short axis; long-axis measurements make reactive nodes look pathological.",

changes.before: "explain": "Omental infarct and epiploic appendagitis are the two self-limiting fat lesions that imitate appendicitis and diverticulitis, and CT separates them confidently. Omental infarct is the larger of the two, typically over 5 cm, heterogeneous and whorled, sited between the colon and the anterior abdominal wall \u2014 most often on the right \u2014 and it is disproportionately a disease of children and of obese adults. Epiploic appendagitis is smaller, oval, under about 5 cm, with a thin hyperattenuating rim and sometimes a central dot representing a thrombosed vein, and it hugs the colonic serosa, usually the sigmoid. Neither needs antibiotics or an operation; both settle over weeks with analgesia. The normal appendix here rules out the phlegmon option. Liposarcoma is a mass with nodular soft tissue components in a patient without acute pain, not an inflamed omental fat lesion of sudden onset.",

changes.before: "explain": "Right-sided diverticulitis is clinically indistinguishable from appendicitis \u2014 same site, same age group, same tenderness \u2014 and it is relatively more common in patients of East and South-East Asian descent, in whom the diverticula tend to be solitary, true and right-sided. CT settles it by showing an inflamed outpouching with surrounding stranding and a demonstrably normal appendix. Most cases respond to antibiotics and supportive care, and the value of making the diagnosis before the operation is that it avoids a needless appendicectomy or, worse, an over-extensive resection of an inflamed caecum that the surgeon cannot distinguish from a tumour at the table. Carcinoma does deserve consideration when the wall thickening is asymmetric and shouldered rather than centred on a diverticulum, particularly in older patients \u2014 but at 32, with a visible inflamed diverticulum, medical treatment with later colonic assessment is the proportionate advice.",

changes.before: "explain": "A long segment of terminal ileum with mural stratification, engorged vasa recta along the mesenteric border and proliferation of the surrounding fat, in a young patient with months of diarrhoea, is ileocolic Crohn disease until proven otherwise. Diagnosis is made by endoscopy and histology, and the imaging job afterwards is mapping \u2014 MR enterography for disease length, activity, strictures, fistulae and abscesses, which spares a young patient repeated CT over decades of follow-up. Infective ileitis from Yersinia, Campylobacter or Salmonella can look identical on a single acute study, which is precisely why the history and the endoscopy matter rather than a repeat scan. Barium studies have been superseded for this indication. The normal appendix in a case like this is a finding to report positively, since it is what keeps the patient off the emergency list.",

changes.before: "explain": "Preserved arterial flow is the classic trap in ovarian torsion. The ovary has a dual supply from the ovarian and uterine arteries, torsion is often intermittent and partial, and venous outflow fails before arterial inflow does \u2014 so Doppler can look deceptively normal in a torted ovary. The diagnosis rests on the grey-scale findings: a unilaterally enlarged oedematous ovary, follicles pushed to the periphery by stromal oedema, an abnormal position of the ovary near the midline or above the uterus, a whirlpool of the twisted pedicle, and often a lead-point cyst or dermoid. Salvage depends on how fast detorsion happens, so this is a telephone call, not a routine referral. CT may be the study that happens to be done first in an undifferentiated abdomen, but ultrasound with Doppler is the test of choice, and a normal appendix does not close the case.",

changes.before: "explain": "Appendicitis is a disease of luminal obstruction, and in a patient over about 50 the thing doing the obstructing may be a neoplasm \u2014 a caecal carcinoma at the appendiceal orifice, or a mucinous neoplasm of the appendix itself. The clue is that the findings extend beyond what appendicitis alone explains: asymmetric caecal wall thickening with shouldered margins rather than symmetrical funnelling of the caecal apex, a soft tissue mass at the base, disproportionate lymph nodes, or a distended mucin-filled appendix with mural calcification. The report should name the concern and recommend colonoscopy or CT after the acute episode has settled, because that recommendation is often the only thing that carries the patient into a cancer pathway. Saying only 'acute appendicitis' in this situation is technically true and clinically incomplete.",

changes.before: "explain": "Children are the ideal ultrasound patients: thin abdominal walls, little intervening fat, and a short distance to the appendix, so a competent operator visualises it in a high proportion of cases. Radiation risk is also at its most consequential in a long life expectancy, which makes ultrasound first the right default. The pathway must not stall there, though. If the appendix is not seen and the child stays symptomatic, the options are a repeat ultrasound in experienced hands, MRI where it is genuinely available and the child will lie still, or CT. Withholding CT from a deteriorating child in order to avoid a dose is a false economy \u2014 perforation, abscess and sepsis are the greater harm. Out-of-hours MRI access is rarely comparable to ultrasound, which is why it cannot be the standing first test.",

changes.before: "explain": "Ultrasound is excellent for stones in the gallbladder \u2014 sensitivity comfortably above 90 per cent for a mobile shadowing echogenic focus \u2014 and poor for stones in the duct, where reported sensitivity is around half or less. The reason is anatomical: the retroduodenal and intrapancreatic segments lie behind gas-filled bowel, and small stones bathed in bile may not shadow at all. So a duct that is dilated with obstructive biochemistry is an indication for direct duct imaging, not for repeating the ultrasound. MRCP is the usual first choice; endoscopic ultrasound is more sensitive for stones under 5 mm where it is available, and ERCP is reserved for treatment rather than diagnosis. CT is a poor stone test, because many calculi are cholesterol-predominant and isodense with bile.",

changes.before: "explain": "The trap sits in the negative Murphy sign. In gangrenous cholecystitis the wall is necrotic and its innervation destroyed, so focal tenderness is often lost \u2014 precisely in the patients who are sickest. Diabetes, age and analgesia compound this. The findings that make the diagnosis are the striated, heterogeneous wall, intraluminal membranes from sloughed mucosa, focal wall defects, and, on CT or contrast-enhanced ultrasound, segments of wall that do not perfuse. It matters because gangrene multiplies the risk of perforation and death and pushes management towards urgent cholecystectomy, or a percutaneous cholecystostomy if the patient is too unwell for theatre. Adenomyomatosis produces comet-tail reverberation from crystals in intramural sinuses in a gallbladder that is not tender, and carcinoma produces focal irregular solid thickening with invasion of the liver interface rather than membranes.",

changes.before: "explain": "Gas in the wall means gas-forming organisms \u2014 commonly Clostridium perfringens or Escherichia coli \u2014 growing in an ischaemic gallbladder. The associations are diabetes and male sex, and roughly half the cases have no stones at all. Mortality is several times that of ordinary calculous cholecystitis and perforation is far more likely, so this is a telephone call, not a report line. Ultrasound is treacherous here: intramural gas produces bright echoes with dirty shadowing and ring-down that can be mistaken for a stone-packed gallbladder or overlying bowel, and if the lumen cannot be resolved at all the correct move is a CT rather than a confident report. Two look-alikes to keep separate. Porcelain gallbladder is mural calcification, dense and cleanly shadowing, with none of the dirty reverberation. Pneumobilia is central and branching, following the ducts towards the hilum.",

changes.before: "explain": "Acalculous cholecystitis is a disease of the critically ill \u2014 burns, sepsis, major trauma, prolonged parenteral nutrition, mechanical ventilation \u2014 driven by bile stasis and gallbladder wall ischaemia, and it gangrenes and perforates more readily than calculous disease. The difficulty is that intensive care itself produces every individual finding: hypoalbuminaemia and positive-pressure ventilation thicken the wall, fluid overload gives pericholecystic fluid, and fasting distends the gallbladder. So the diagnosis is a judgement built on the whole picture, supported where needed by cholescintigraphy showing non-filling of the gallbladder at 60 minutes with morphine augmentation, or by a wall perfusion defect on CT or contrast-enhanced ultrasound. Percutaneous cholecystostomy is frequently chosen over surgery because these patients tolerate anaesthesia and laparotomy badly, and drainage buys time for the underlying illness to be treated.",

changes.before: "explain": "A thick gallbladder wall is a finding, not a diagnosis, and the list of causes that are not cholecystitis is long: the physiologically contracted post-prandial gallbladder, hypoalbuminaemia of any cause, right heart failure and raised central venous pressure, cirrhosis and portal hypertension, acute hepatitis, renal failure, pancreatitis, adenomyomatosis and carcinoma. In cirrhosis the wall is thick for two reasons at once \u2014 low oncotic pressure and venous congestion \u2014 and Doppler may show varices within it. What should raise suspicion instead is focal rather than diffuse thickening, an irregular solid component, loss of the interface with adjacent liver, and internal vascularity, all of which point at gallbladder carcinoma. Writing this out matters: an unqualified line about a thickened wall in a cirrhotic patient generates surgical referrals and occasionally an operation that nobody needed.",

changes.before: "explain": "Pneumobilia is the classic MRCP mimic after sphincterotomy, a biliary-enteric anastomosis or stent placement. Two features separate it from a stone. Gas rises to the non-dependent surface \u2014 anterior in a supine patient \u2014 while a stone falls to the dependent wall; and gas blooms on gradient-echo sequences because of its susceptibility effect, whereas a stone does not. If real doubt persists, gas is unmistakable on CT. Other MRCP traps are worth carrying: pulsation of the right hepatic artery crossing the common hepatic duct makes a linear void, susceptibility from clips or a metal stent can obliterate a whole segment of duct, stones under about 5 mm are readily missed, and a calculus impacted at the ampulla can be mistaken for normal distal tapering. When the clinical suspicion is strong and MRCP is negative, endoscopic ultrasound is the more sensitive next step.",

changes.before: "explain": "Stricture morphology is one of the few reliably discriminating observations in biliary imaging. Benign strictures are the product of diffuse fibrosis and taper gradually with preserved, concentric mucosal contour; the usual causes are chronic pancreatitis, previous surgery or instrumentation, ischaemia after transplantation, IgG4-related disease and passed stones. Malignant strictures are the product of a growing mass and end abruptly, with irregular shouldered margins, asymmetry, a long segment of involvement, associated periductal soft tissue and enhancement, and often upstream ductal wall thickening. Neither pattern is absolute, and brush cytology has poor sensitivity, so a persistent stricture with a negative brushing is not cleared \u2014 repeat sampling, cholangioscopy or resection may still be needed. State the length, the margin, and the presence or absence of enhancing soft tissue, because those three data points drive the next decision.",

Benign strictures are the product of diffuse fibrosis and taper gradually with preserved, concentric mucosal contour; the usual causes are chronic pancreatitis, previous surgery or instrumentation, ischaemia after transplantation, IgG4-related disease and passed stones. Malignant strictures are the product of a growing mass and end abruptly, with irregular shouldered margins, asymmetry, a long segment of involvement, associated periductal soft tissue and enhancement, and often upstream ductal wall thickening. Neither pattern is absolute, and brush cytology has poor sensitivity, so a persistent stricture with a negative brushing is not cleared — repeat sampling, cholangioscopy or resection may still be needed. State the length, the margin, and the presence or absence of enhancing soft tissue, because those three data points drive the next decision.",

changes.before: "explain": "VI-RADS rests on seeing a continuous low-signal muscularis propria, and that line only behaves predictably in a moderately distended bladder. Empty the bladder and the wall folds on itself: it looks thickened everywhere, a small sessile tumour disappears into the folds, and the dark muscle line becomes impossible to follow. Fill it too far and the wall is stretched thin, a papillary tumour is pressed flat and loses its stalk, and the patient cannot lie still for a diffusion series. The practical instruction is to void, then wait one to two hours, or to drink a measured volume beforehand. If the study is done at either extreme, say so in the report \u2014 a VI-RADS category assigned on an under-distended bladder is not the same evidence as one assigned on a good study.",

changes.before: "explain": "Two: the small bowel at 3.6 cm and the caecum at 11.0 cm. The transverse colon at 5.2 cm is within normal limits. The 3/6/9 rule \u2014 3 cm for small bowel, 6 cm for colon, 9 cm for caecum \u2014 is a crude but durable bedside aid, and the caecal figure is the one that carries urgency. By Laplace's law, wall tension rises with radius, so the caecum, the widest and thinnest-walled segment, is where an obstructed colon perforates first, typically without any warning from the pain score. A caecum beyond about 12 cm is widely treated as demanding decompression. Radiographic measurement is approximate: magnification, projection and overlapping loops all distort it, so confirm on CT, where you can also assess wall enhancement and look for the cause.",

changes.before: "explain": "Adhesions cause most small bowel obstruction in adults with previous surgery, and they are diagnosed by what is absent: an abrupt transition with nothing at it \u2014 no mass, no wall thickening, no hernia, no intussusception, no inflammatory process. That makes the diagnosis a duty rather than a shrug. Before accepting it you must inspect every hernial orifice including femoral and obturator, look for a beak within the mesentery suggesting an internal hernia, and check for a lesion at the transition on thin reformats. Ileus is excluded here by the collapsed distal bowel and colon: an ileus dilates everything without a calibre change. Gallstone ileus has its own triad of pneumobilia, obstruction and an ectopic stone. The final clause \u2014 no signs of strangulation \u2014 is the part the surgeon reads first, because it is what permits a trial of conservative management.",

changes.before: "explain": "The small bowel faeces sign is gas bubbles suspended in particulate debris within dilated small bowel, produced by stasis, water resorption and bacterial overgrowth in a segment whose contents have not moved. Its practical value is topographical: it sits just proximal to the transition point, so when the transition is hard to find, follow the faecalised segment distally and it will usually take you there. It also tells you the obstruction is not brand new. What it is not is an ischaemia sign, and reading it as one leads to overcalling. It appears in Crohn disease, in some chronic strictures and occasionally without obstruction at all. Judge urgency on wall enhancement, mesenteric oedema, closed-loop configuration and the patient's physiology, and use the faeces sign for what it is good at \u2014 finding the level.",

changes.before: "explain": "A closed loop is a segment obstructed at two points close together, usually by a single adhesive band or a hernial neck, and it is the configuration most likely to strangulate because the mesentery is caught in the same twist. Recognise it by the shape \u2014 a C or U-shaped, fluid-filled, disproportionately dilated loop \u2014 by two transition points converging at one site, and by mesenteric vessels stretched and radiating towards that point, sometimes with a whirl. Then look specifically for the viability signs: reduced or absent wall enhancement, mural thickening, mesenteric oedema and fluid, ascites, pneumatosis, portal venous gas. The report is not the communication. A closed loop with reduced enhancement is a phone call in minutes, because the interval between venous occlusion and transmural infarction is measured in hours and the operation is different if the bowel has to be resected.",

changes.before: "explain": "The sequence is forced by logic. First establish that bowel is genuinely obstructed rather than merely dilated: dilated proximal bowel with collapsed distal bowel and colon, against the 3/6/9 calibre limits. Second, find the transition point by following the dilated loops to where calibre changes, using coronal reformats, since the level determines whether this is a small or large bowel problem. Third, work out what is at the transition \u2014 adhesion, hernia, tumour, intussusception, volvulus, gallstone, inflammatory stricture \u2014 because the cause decides whether conservative management is even an option. Fourth, and never omitted, assess viability: wall enhancement, mural thickness, mesenteric fat and fluid, pneumatosis, portal venous gas. Viability comes last in the reading order but first in the conversation with the surgeon, because it is the finding that changes the timing of the operation rather than only its nature.",

changes.before: "explain": "A competent ileocaecal valve converts a distal colonic obstruction into a closed loop between the valve and the tumour. Nothing can escape proximally into the ileum or distally past the tumour, so the colon \u2014 and above all the caecum \u2014 takes the whole pressure. Because wall tension rises with radius, the caecum is the segment that ruptures, and it can do so with a deceptively comfortable abdomen. Paradoxically, the absence of small bowel dilatation is therefore the worrying feature, not the reassuring one: decompression into dilated small bowel means an incompetent valve and a lower immediate perforation risk. Report the caecal diameter as a number, comment on caecal wall enhancement and any pericaecal fluid or pneumatosis, and flag it for urgent decompression, whether by stent, defunctioning stoma or resection. This is not an elective list problem.",

changes.before: "explain": "Sigmoid volvulus is a disease of the elderly, the immobile and the chronically constipated, and the classic radiograph is an enormously dilated inverted U arising from the pelvis, its apex often reaching above the transverse colon and pointing towards the right upper quadrant, with absent rectal gas. CT confirms it with a whirl of twisted mesentery and two beaks at the point of torsion, and \u2014 crucially \u2014 assesses viability. With enhancing wall and no free gas, first-line management is endoscopic detorsion with a flatus tube left in place, which succeeds in most patients and converts an emergency into a planned procedure. Recurrence is high, so elective sigmoidectomy is usually considered afterwards. Perforation, peritonitis or CT evidence of ischaemia overrides all of this and sends the patient straight to theatre. Contrast enema is diagnostic at best and has been overtaken by CT.",

changes.before: "explain": "Caecal volvulus needs a congenitally mobile caecum on an unfused mesentery, so it affects a much younger population than sigmoid volvulus. The giveaways are the empty right iliac fossa, the dilated caecum displaced towards the left upper quadrant, dilated small bowel proximal to it because the obstruction sits at the ileocaecal level, and a collapsed distal colon. On CT, look for the whirl of the twisted ileocolic pedicle and then for wall enhancement. The management diverges sharply from sigmoid volvulus: endoscopic reduction is technically difficult, frequently fails and recurs, so the answer is operative \u2014 right hemicolectomy where the patient can take it, caecopexy or caecostomy where they cannot. Say the diagnosis explicitly in the report rather than describing a distended loop, because the word caecal is what routes the patient to theatre instead of to endoscopy.",

changes.before: "explain": "The distinction rests on one question: is there a transition point? An ileus dilates the whole gut uniformly, small bowel and colon together, with gas carried through to the rectum and no calibre change; mechanical obstruction dilates proximally and collapses distally around a discrete transition. Ileus follows surgery, electrolyte disturbance \u2014 especially hypokalaemia \u2014 opiates, sepsis, retroperitoneal inflammation and spinal injury, and it is treated by removing the cause. The trap is early post-operative mechanical obstruction, from an internal hernia or a tight closure, which can masquerade as a slow ileus and only declares itself when someone looks specifically for a transition point. So report the absence of a transition as a positive finding, and set a threshold: if the picture does not settle over the next couple of days, or the patient becomes tender or tachycardic, rescan and look again.",

changes.before: "explain": "Direction of flow separates the two. Portal blood runs from the hilum outwards, so portal venous gas is peripheral, fine and branching, typically reaching within 2 cm of the liver capsule and favouring the left lobe in a supine patient. Bile flows towards the hilum, so pneumobilia is central, coarser, and clusters around the porta \u2014 the expected finding after sphincterotomy, a biliary-enteric anastomosis or an incompetent sphincter. Portal venous gas together with pneumatosis in a septic patient is bowel infarction until proven otherwise and warrants immediate surgical discussion. The nuance to hold alongside it is that pneumatosis on its own is not always ischaemic: it occurs in chronic lung disease, with corticosteroids and some chemotherapy agents, after endoscopy, and in connective tissue disease. The company it keeps, and the patient, decide the meaning.",

changes.before: "explain": "Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction is massive colonic dilatation with no mechanical cause, typically in an elderly inpatient after surgery, trauma or acute illness, and often with electrolyte disturbance, opiates or anticholinergics contributing. The distinguishing features on CT are gas carried right through into the rectum and the absence of any transition point \u2014 a sigmoid volvulus would show a whirl and beaks, and a tumour would show a shouldered stricture. First-line treatment is conservative: stop the offending drugs, correct potassium and magnesium, decompress nasogastrically, mobilise. Neostigmine under cardiac monitoring is effective in many patients, with colonoscopic decompression where it fails or is contraindicated. Report the caecal diameter and wall enhancement each time, because a caecum beyond about 12 cm, or one with pneumatosis, thinning or pericaecal fluid, is the trigger for escalation to surgery.",

changes.before: "explain": "When there is no history of previous surgery, the transition point is far more likely to be a hernia than an adhesion, so the hernial orifices deserve a deliberate pass on the coronal images every time. The obturator hernia is the one most often missed: it occurs in thin, elderly, often multiparous women, the bowel passes through the obturator canal between pectineus and obturator externus, and compression of the obturator nerve produces pain referred to the medial thigh or knee \u2014 the Howship-Romberg sign. The neck is narrow and rigid, so strangulation is common and the reported mortality is high; this is an urgent operation, not a conservative trial. Check the femoral canals, the umbilicus, old incisions, and the mesenteric windows for internal hernias in the same sweep. Naming the hernia in the report changes both the urgency and the surgical approach.",

changes.before: "explain": "The homunculus is the whole argument. The leg and perineum sit on the medial surface at the paracentral lobule, and that surface, together with the genu and body of the corpus callosum and the medial frontal cortex, is anterior cerebral artery territory carried by the pericallosal and callosomarginal branches. Leg-dominant weakness with a spared face is therefore ACA until proven otherwise, and the abulia comes from the medial frontal and cingulate involvement. The middle cerebral artery's superior division supplies the lateral convexity, so it gives face and arm weakness with sparing of the leg \u2014 the mirror image. Heubner's recurrent artery supplies the caudate head and the anterior limb of the internal capsule; it produces a small deep infarct with facio-brachial weakness and dysarthria, not a strip of medial cortex. The anterior choroidal artery supplies the posterior limb of the internal capsule, optic tract and medial temporal structures, classically hemiplegia with hemianaesthesia and hemianopia. When you see a medial strip, look next at the A1 segments and the anterior communicating complex, because a single dominant A1 can infarct both medial hemispheres at once.",

changes.before: "explain": "There are two borderzones and they mean different things. The external, or cortical, borderzone lies between the surface branches of the anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries and infarcts as a wedge running from the ventricle to the cortex; it is often embolic, with hypoperfusion impairing washout of emboli. The internal, or deep, borderzone lies between the lenticulostriate perforators from below and the long medullary branches descending from the cortical arteries above, in the corona radiata and centrum semiovale. It infarcts as a linear string of small lesions parallel to the lateral ventricle \u2014 the rosary bead appearance \u2014 and it is the most haemodynamic of all stroke patterns. A normal cortical ribbon argues against embolism, and diffusion restriction argues against old small vessel disease, which would be T2 hyperintense without restriction. The management consequence is the point: this patient needs perfusion assessment and an urgent decision about revascularising the carotid, plus avoidance of further hypotension, not simply another antiplatelet.",

changes.before: "explain": "The anterior choroidal artery arises from the supraclinoid internal carotid just distal to the posterior communicating artery and runs backwards along the optic tract into the temporal horn. Its territory is small but strategically dense: the posterior limb of the internal capsule (its inferior and posterior part), the optic tract, the lateral geniculate nucleus, the medial temporal structures including the uncus and part of the hippocampus, and the choroid plexus of the temporal horn. That gives three of the five listed. The caudate head belongs to the recurrent artery of Heubner and the medial lenticulostriates, and the occipital cortex belongs to the posterior cerebral artery. The reason to hold this territory in mind is the classical triad it produces \u2014 contralateral hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia and homonymous hemianopia \u2014 from a lesion no larger than a lacune. If you see a small capsular infarct and the patient has a field defect, look for optic tract and geniculate involvement rather than assuming a second lesion.",

changes.before: "explain": "Hearing loss is the discriminator. The internal auditory (labyrinthine) artery usually arises from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, so AICA is the one posterior circulation territory in which cochlear and vestibular failure sits alongside brainstem signs. Add lower motor neurone facial weakness from the facial nucleus in the caudal pons, ataxia from the middle cerebellar peduncle and flocculus, and crossed sensory loss from the spinothalamic tract, and the lateral pontine syndrome is complete. PICA gives the lateral medullary syndrome: vertigo, hoarseness and dysphagia from the nucleus ambiguus, Horner syndrome, crossed sensory loss \u2014 but hearing is preserved and the facial weakness, if any, is not of lower motor neurone type. SCA gives ataxia, dysarthria and sometimes a contralateral fourth nerve palsy, without hearing loss. A paramedian perforator gives a ventral pontine syndrome with contralateral hemiparesis and no vestibulocochlear features. In practice, sudden isolated deafness with vertigo in a vasculopath is an AICA warning and deserves urgent posterior circulation imaging rather than a labyrinthitis label.",

changes.before: "explain": "The deep venous system is a fixed chain and knowing it lets you predict which structures swell when one link fails. The thalamostriate and septal veins meet at the venous angle behind the foramen of Monro to form the paired internal cerebral veins, which run back in the velum interpositum. They join the basal veins of Rosenthal, carrying blood from the medial temporal lobes and midbrain, to form the great cerebral vein of Galen beneath the splenium. The vein of Galen meets the inferior sagittal sinus to become the straight sinus, which runs in the falco-tentorial junction to the confluence of sinuses, then out through the transverse and sigmoid sinuses to the internal jugular vein. Thrombosis anywhere from the internal cerebral veins to the straight sinus produces bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia oedema, often haemorrhagic \u2014 the venous mimic of the artery of Percheron. Thrombosis further downstream, in a transverse or sigmoid sinus, is far more often silent or presents with raised pressure, because the cortical veins and the opposite side can compensate.",

changes.before: "explain": "The anatomy explains the clinical pattern. In the cavernous sinus the oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic and maxillary nerves are embedded in the lateral dural wall, insulated to some degree from what is happening in the venous channel itself. The abducens nerve is the exception: it runs free inside the sinus, immediately lateral to the cavernous internal carotid artery. Anything that expands or infiltrates the venous compartment \u2014 tumour, thrombosis, a carotid\u2013cavernous fistula, inflammatory pseudotumour \u2014 therefore tends to strike the sixth nerve first, and an isolated abducens palsy with an otherwise quiet orbit should send you to thin-section coronal images of the cavernous sinuses before anywhere else. In the superior orbital fissure the sixth nerve is inside the annulus of Zinn, not outside it, and a fissure lesion would rarely spare the third and fourth nerves. Meckel's cave contains the trigeminal ganglion, not the sixth nerve, and the internal auditory canal carries the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves. Do not forget raised intracranial pressure, which stretches the sixth nerve at Dorello's canal and is a false localising sign.",

changes.before: "explain": "The jugular foramen transmits the glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves, along with the internal jugular vein and the inferior petrosal sinus; the hypoglossal canal, just anteromedial and inferior to it in the occipital bone, transmits the twelfth nerve alone. A lesion occupying both therefore threatens four nerves \u2014 IX, X, XI and XII \u2014 which together make up the classical Collet\u2013Sicard pattern, and the clinical consequence is a patient who cannot protect their airway. That is why this specific extension deserves an explicit sentence in your report rather than a general statement about skull base involvement. Keeping the neighbouring openings straight is worth the effort: the internal auditory meatus carries VII and VIII, the foramen ovale carries V3, the foramen rotundum carries V2, the optic canal carries II with the ophthalmic artery, and the superior orbital fissure carries III, IV, V1 and VI. When a mass sits at the pars nervosa or pars vascularis, look also for the vertical segment of the carotid and for a high jugular bulb before anyone contemplates biopsy.",

changes.before: "explain": "Venous infarcts announce themselves by disobeying arterial boundaries, by bleeding early, and by having oedema disproportionate to the infarct. Once you suspect one, work out which vein and then look at the sinus it empties into. The vein of Labb\u00e9 drains the lateral temporal convexity backwards into the transverse sinus, so a transverse or sigmoid sinus thrombosis produces exactly this temporal haemorrhagic lesion, sometimes with a rapid decline as the temporal lobe swells against the tentorium. The vein of Trolard runs upwards to the superior sagittal sinus and matches parasagittal high convexity lesions, which is why superior sagittal sinus thrombosis gives bilateral parasagittal haemorrhages. Rosenthal's basal vein and the internal cerebral veins belong to the deep system and produce thalamic and basal ganglia oedema instead. The next step here is a dedicated venogram and anticoagulation, which is given even in the presence of venous haemorrhage \u2014 the bleeding is a consequence of the outflow obstruction, not a contraindication to relieving it.",

changes.before: "explain": "It is tempting to call two lesions two events, but the posterior cerebral artery supplies both cortex and deep grey, and a single P2 occlusion can take out the calcarine cortex and the lateral thalamus together. The thalamic supply is regional: the tuberothalamic artery from the posterior communicating artery, the paramedian thalamoperforators from P1, the thalamogeniculate branches from P2 to the posterolateral thalamus, and the posterior choroidal arteries to the pulvinar and geniculate bodies. A posterolateral thalamic plus medial occipital pattern is the P2 signature. The variant that changes management is a fetal posterior cerebral artery, present in roughly a fifth to a quarter of hemispheres, in which the PCA arises from the internal carotid through a dominant posterior communicating artery with a hypoplastic or absent P1. In that patient an occipital infarct is a carotid territory event, so the carotid bifurcation, not the vertebrobasilar system, is where the workup belongs \u2014 and it also matters when planning any carotid intervention.",

changes.before: "explain": "Meckel's cave is a cerebrospinal fluid-filled dural pouch in the petrous apex holding the trigeminal ganglion, and it is a junction box: the ophthalmic division leaves through the superior orbital fissure, the maxillary division through the foramen rotundum, and the mandibular division through the foramen ovale into the masticator space. Because the patient has both sensory loss and weakness of chewing, the motor fibres travelling with V3 are involved, so the foramen ovale is the route to follow. The specific sign to hunt for is denervation of the masseter, temporalis and pterygoids \u2014 oedematous and T2 bright in the subacute phase, fatty and atrophic later \u2014 which can be the only clue that a small perineural tumour is present. Perineural spread from a skin or parotid malignancy classically travels this way, and it upstages disease and changes the radiotherapy field, so it is worth an explicit statement in the report. The maxillary route matters for palatal and midface tumours, and the facial and lower cranial nerve routes belong to different clinical pictures altogether.",

changes.before: "explain": "The single whole-body film \u2014 the babygram \u2014 fails because it images most of the skeleton off-axis, at the wrong exposure, with the divergent beam obliquing the metaphyses and ribs it most needs to show. The standard survey is a set of individually collimated projections: two views of the skull, lateral cervical and thoracolumbar spine, frontal chest with left and right oblique rib views, abdomen and pelvis, and separate frontal views of humeri, forearms, hands, femora, tibiae and feet. Coning and correct positioning are what make a classic metaphyseal lesion visible at all. CT delivers a dose that cannot be justified as a screening survey, though targeted CT of head and, with reformats, of skull and ribs has a role. Whole-body MRI complements the survey by finding marrow and soft-tissue injury, but it misses metaphyseal and rib fractures and does not replace it.",
changes.after: "explain": "The single whole-body film — the babygram — fails because it images most of the skeleton off-axis, at the wrong exposure, with the divergent beam obliquing the metaphyses and ribs it most needs to show. The standard survey is a set of individually collimated projections: two views of the skull, lateral cervical and thoracolumbar spine, frontal chest with left and right oblique rib views, abdomen and pelvis, and separate frontal views of humeri, forearms, hands, femora, tibiae and feet. Coning and correct positioning are what make a classic metaphyseal lesion visible at all. CT delivers a dose that cannot be justified as a screening survey, though targeted CT of head and, with reformats, of skull and ribs has a role. Whole-body MRI complements the survey by finding marrow and soft-tissue injury, but it misses metaphyseal and rib fractures and does not replace it.",

changes.before: "explain": "A normal first survey does not exclude skeletal injury, because the two most specific fractures are the two hardest to see acutely. Undisplaced posterior rib fractures and classic metaphyseal lesions frequently become visible only as subperiosteal new bone and callus appear, and the accepted interval for that is eleven to fourteen days. The repeat is limited: chest with obliques, long bones, and any region of concern. Skull films are generally omitted, since fractures of the skull heal without callus and a repeat film adds nothing. Scintigraphy is sensitive for rib and shaft injury but is poor at the skull and at symmetrical metaphyseal disease, and it cannot characterise what it detects. Repeating on the day of discharge, if that is day four, wastes the examination \u2014 timing is the whole point.",

changes.before: "answer": "Imaging can place each fracture in a broad range \u2014 acute, healing or old \u2014 and can state that fractures of differing ages are present, but it cannot date any of them to a particular day, and a skull fracture cannot be dated at all because it heals without callus.",
changes.after: "answer": "Imaging can place each fracture in a broad range — acute, healing or old — and can state that fractures of differing ages are present, but it cannot date any of them to a particular day, and a skull fracture cannot be dated at all because it heals without callus.",

changes.before: "explain": "Fourteen days is the upper limit of the conventional eleven to fourteen day window, and the reason for both ends is physiological rather than administrative. Repeat too early and subperiosteal new bone has not yet mineralised enough to be seen on a plain film; leave it too long and a child is exposed to continuing risk while the investigation waits, and some rib callus begins to remodel. The repeat typically finds fractures the first survey missed in a meaningful minority of cases, chiefly posterior ribs and classic metaphyseal lesions, and it also reclassifies apparent findings as normal variants, which protects families as much as it protects children. It is limited rather than full \u2014 chest with obliques, long bones, and any site of concern \u2014 and the skull is normally left out because skull fractures do not heal with callus.",

changes.before: "explain": "Everything here places the lesion in the carotid space: the parapharyngeal fat pushed forwards, and a mass sitting between the two carotid arteries at the bifurcation. Splaying of the internal from the external carotid is the signature of a paraganglioma arising in the carotid body, and the avid enhancement with flow voids fits. That vascularity is exactly why percutaneous biopsy is the wrong move \u2014 the diagnosis is made on imaging, and the patient goes on to catecholamine screening, assessment for multicentric disease, and genetic testing for succinate dehydrogenase mutations. A vagal paraganglioma sits higher and pushes the internal carotid anteromedially rather than splaying it, while a vagal schwannoma displaces both vessels together and enhances less avidly; both remain reasonable considerations until the splaying is seen. A cystic lesion is excluded by the enhancement, and a nodal metastasis would not sit between the vessels.",

changes.before: "explain": "Four divided by fourteen is 0.286, so 29 per cent of the airway remains \u2014 a figure worth calculating because it is the number that changes what happens in the next hour. The instinct on seeing a deep neck collection is to measure the abscess; the anaesthetist needs the airway. A report that leads with the calibre and the level of narrowing, the degree of laryngeal or tracheal deviation, and whether the epiglottis and supraglottis are involved, will be acted on faster than one that opens with the volume of pus. Two other measurements matter as much: how far the collection extends craniocaudally, and whether it reaches below the thoracic inlet, since descent into the posterior mediastinum turns a neck problem into a thoracic emergency. Say plainly if the airway looks unsafe for a supine, sedated examination.",

changes.before: "explain": "Phlegmon and abscess are two points on one continuum, and the CT distinction is what decides between a ward and a theatre. Phlegmon is oedematous, infiltrated tissue that enhances more or less uniformly with stranding of the fat and no non-enhancing centre; it is treated with antibiotics and observed. An abscess has a definable rim that enhances around a centre that does not, and gas within it settles the matter. CT is not infallible in that judgement \u2014 small non-enhancing areas of necrosis inside a phlegmon are over-called as abscesses, which is one reason a collection under about 2 cm is often managed medically at first. Whatever the wording, the airway comes first in the report, the craniocaudal extent second, and the vessels third: look for thrombus in the internal jugular vein, which with septic pulmonary emboli would raise the possibility of Lemierre syndrome.",

changes.before: "explain": "Cutaneous squamous carcinoma of the face and adenoid cystic carcinoma are the two tumours that most reliably travel along nerves, and they can do so years after the primary was treated and with clear margins at the time. The direct signs are nerve thickening, abnormal enhancement, loss of the fat that outlines a nerve at its foramen, and widening or erosion of the foramen itself; fat-saturated post-contrast sequences make them visible. The indirect sign is denervation of the muscles the nerve supplies, which passes through an acute oedematous phase, bright on T2 and enhancing, into chronic fatty atrophy \u2014 the appearance here. Because the auriculotemporal nerve links V3 to the facial nerve, always follow both, and look at the geniculate ganglion and the stylomastoid foramen before concluding. Report the most proximal level involved, since that dictates whether surgery can reach it.",

changes.before: "population_note": "Partial original source surface from one professionally trained female singer during sustained Stiff phonation. This is not swallowing, VFSS, aspiration assessment, a normal atlas or the anatomy of the patient being reported. All 29,326 original triangles, four source components and 328 open boundary edges are retained in their exact original STL coordinates and face order. No fit, centering, smoothing, capping, repair, decimation or fragment deletion. Neutral display colour and averaged display normals are not photographic tissue appearance. Original Blender 3.4.1 STL has no patient direction, coordinate-system or unit declaration. Cameras refer only to source coordinates. The paper provides nominal millimetre-scale context; source STL calibration and anatomical directions remain unverified. The matching published MR array has nominal 0.8 mm native acquisition resolution and a zero-filled export pitch 0.3839285671710968 (nominal 0.4 mm in the paper). This export grid does not increase acquired anatomical resolution. The MRI primary NRRD geometry declares LPS. Inherited NIfTI srow strings conflict in x/z directions even after LPS to RAS convention conversion. Fixed-sign image correspondence favours an LPS hypothesis for this STL, but producer transform and segmentation mask are absent. No MRI overlay or source-volume registration is presented or approved. Phase 01 is the authors\u2019 maximum glottal-opening bin. Ten acoustic phase bins aggregate an oscillatory cycle over a 5 min 20 s sustained-phonation acquisition; they are not consecutive independent live frames or a swallowing timeline. Audio-to-volume sample timing and MRI-to-upright high-speed video correspondence remain unverified. Threshold-segmented air\u2013tissue interface only. Individual cartilage, vocal-fold tissue layers, ligaments, muscles, mucosa, vessels and nerves are not independently labelled. Source surface ends truncate the visible airway extent. No physiological function, patient diagnosis, complete reporting anatomy or clinical/commercial fidelity is established. Selected complete ZIP member CRC32 and local SHA256 were verified; publisher archive size/checksum remained stable before/after range acquisition. The whole 5.23 GB ZIP MD5 was not independently verified and no HTTP entity tag was available. changes.before: "explain": "The swirl sign is fresh, unretracted blood \u2014 still liquid and therefore lower in attenuation than the clotted blood around it \u2014 and it means the bleeding has not stopped. In an extradural haematoma from a torn middle meningeal artery, that is a surgical emergency: the collection can double in an hour, and the lucid interval described here is the classical prelude to rapid decompensation. The shape and the fracture together make the compartment clear. Extradural blood is biconvex because it has to strip the dura off the inner table against its firm attachment at the sutures, so it does not cross a suture, though it can cross the midline and the tentorium because it is not bounded by dural reflections. Subdural blood is the reverse: crescentic, crossing sutures freely, but halted at the falx and tentorium. Chronic collections are uniformly low in attenuation without the irregular internal swirls, and artefact from bone runs as linear streaks across the whole slice rather than sitting inside the clot.",

changes.before: "explain": "Two anatomical rules do almost all the work in the extra-axial compartment, and they are complementary rather than competing. The dura is two layers: an outer periosteal layer fused to the inner table and adherent at the sutures, and an inner meningeal layer that folds inwards to form the falx and tentorium. Blood in the extradural space lifts the periosteal layer off the bone and is arrested where that layer is tethered, at the sutures; nothing stops it crossing the falx or tentorium, because those structures lie deep to it. Blood in the subdural space slides under the sutures without difficulty but meets the falx and tentorium head on. So crossing a suture argues subdural; crossing the midline argues extradural. Neither rule is absolute \u2014 a fracture that runs through a suture and diastases it lets extradural blood across \u2014 which is why shape, the presence of a fracture and the clinical story are read together. Look for interhemispheric or tentorial layering, which is subdural blood in profile and easily mistaken for subarachnoid.",
