changes.before: "explain": "The sequence is driven by what happens to the haemoglobin iron and by whether it is inside or outside intact red cells. Hyperacute, within the first day, the clot is oxyhaemoglobin and diamagnetic: isointense to slightly hypointense on T1 and bright on T2, essentially looking like water with a rim. Acute, roughly days one to three, oxygen is stripped to deoxyhaemoglobin, which is paramagnetic but sequestered inside cells, so T2 goes dark while T1 stays middling. Early subacute, from about day three, deoxyhaemoglobin oxidises to intracellular methaemoglobin: T1 becomes bright, T2 stays dark. Late subacute, from about a week to a month, the cells lyse and methaemoglobin becomes extracellular, so both T1 and T2 are bright \u2014 the easiest stage to recognise. Chronic, beyond a month, iron is stored as haemosiderin and ferritin in macrophages at the rim, dark on T1 and T2 and blooming heavily on gradient echo and susceptibility imaging. The practical use is dating: a haematoma that does not follow this progression, or that has non-haemorrhagic enhancing tissue within it, should raise the question of an underlying tumour or malformation.",

changes.before: "explain": "The clot points at the hole. Blood centred in the anterior interhemispheric fissure, especially with a haematoma in the gyrus rectus or blood tracking into the septum pellucidum and lateral ventricles, indicates the anterior communicating complex. Blood filling one sylvian fissure with a temporal haematoma indicates a middle cerebral bifurcation aneurysm. Blood in the suprasellar and ambient cisterns on one side, particularly with a third nerve palsy, indicates a posterior communicating origin aneurysm. Blood predominantly in the fourth ventricle and around the foramen magnum indicates a posterior inferior cerebellar artery aneurysm. Saying which one you favour makes the angiogram faster and the interventional plan sharper. The complication to flag with intraventricular extension is acute hydrocephalus, which can develop within hours and is reversible with a drain \u2014 so look every time at the temporal horns and the third ventricle. Beyond that, warn about rebleeding before securing, and delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm from about day four to day fourteen.",

changes.after: "prompt": "An arteriovenous malformation has a nidus measuring 4.2 cm in maximum diameter, lies within the left precentral gyrus, and drains through a subependymal vein into the internal cerebral vein. Give its Spetzler–Martin grade. Answer as a whole number.",

changes.before: "explain": "The Spetzler\u2013Martin scale sums three components. Size scores 1 for a nidus under 3 cm, 2 for 3 to 6 cm and 3 for over 6 cm, so 4.2 cm scores 2. Eloquence of adjacent brain scores 1 if present and 0 if not; the precentral gyrus is eloquent, along with sensory cortex, language cortex, visual cortex, the internal capsule, thalamus, hypothalamus, brainstem, cerebellar peduncles and deep cerebellar nuclei, so that adds 1. Venous drainage scores 1 if any component is deep and 0 if it is entirely superficial; drainage into the internal cerebral vein is deep, so that adds 1 more. Total 4. The scale predicts surgical morbidity, and grades 4 and 5 are usually managed conservatively or with staged embolisation and radiosurgery rather than primary resection. Your report should therefore state each component explicitly rather than only the total, and add the features that carry independent bleeding risk: prior haemorrhage, an intranidal or flow-related aneurysm, venous stenosis and exclusively deep drainage.",

changes.before: "explain": "Two lesions, only one of which bleeds. The caput medusae of small medullary veins draining into a single large collecting vein is a developmental venous anomaly, an anatomical variant of normal venous drainage rather than a malformation with a shunt. It carries essentially no bleeding risk of its own, and crucially it drains normal brain, so occluding or resecting it causes venous infarction \u2014 which is why the correct action is to leave it and to say so plainly in the report. The lesion with the mixed-signal popcorn core and the complete haemosiderin rim is a cavernous malformation, and cavernomas are the things that bleed. They are associated with venous anomalies often enough that finding one should prompt a careful search for the other. If surgery is contemplated, the surgeon must preserve the draining vein. An arteriovenous malformation would show enlarged feeding arteries, a compact nidus and early venous filling on angiography, none of which is described here.",

changes.before: "explain": "Acute extravasated blood measures around 50 to 70 Hounsfield units and then loses roughly 1.5 units a day as the clot breaks down, so somewhere between about one and three weeks it passes through the attenuation of cortex and becomes invisible on standard brain windows. The trap is real: the scan looks unremarkable until you notice the secondary signs \u2014 effaced sulci on one side, inward displacement of the grey\u2013white interface, a cortex that appears abnormally thick, midline shift out of keeping with any visible lesion. Widening the window compresses the greyscale of the brain and lets the collection separate from cortex; comparing the two hemispheres on the same slice is the other half of the trick. If doubt persists, MRI is definitive because subacute blood is bright on T1, and a contrast-enhanced CT shows the enhancing displaced cortical veins. Bilateral isodense collections are the hardest of all, since there is no shift and no asymmetry to alert you \u2014 look for the absent sulci at the vertex.",

changes.before: "explain": "The attenuation of blood on CT is driven mostly by the protein in haemoglobin, so it falls with the haemoglobin concentration. At a haemoglobin of around 80 to 100 g/L, fresh blood can measure close to grey matter, and below that it can look frankly hypodense, meaning an acute subdural haematoma in a profoundly anaemic patient can be reported as chronic or missed altogether. Density alone therefore never dates a collection; you read it alongside the history, the shape, and the presence of a fluid\u2013fluid level or a mixed-density clot, which suggests active bleeding or rebleeding into an older collection. A hygroma is genuinely cerebrospinal fluid density, near zero, typically after trauma or shunting, and it lacks the internal complexity of chronic haematoma. An empyema is usually loculated with an enhancing membrane and restricted diffusion, with a septic patient attached. Coagulopathy is the other setting that changes appearance, producing unclotted low-density blood layered against denser clot.",

changes.before: "explain": "Susceptibility-weighted imaging exploits the phase difference between paramagnetic blood products and surrounding tissue and is substantially more sensitive to microbleeds than conventional gradient echo, which is itself far more sensitive than CT. In an elderly patient with a lobar haemorrhage, that sensitivity is what turns a single event into a pattern: strictly lobar microbleeds with deep sparing and cortical superficial siderosis fulfil elements of the Boston criteria version 2.0 for probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy, and cortical superficial siderosis in particular predicts recurrent lobar haemorrhage. That is exactly the evidence a cardiologist needs when weighing atrial fibrillation against bleeding risk. The interpretive caveats are worth stating in the report. Blooming makes every lesion look larger than it is and the apparent size varies with echo time and field strength, so counts are not comparable between scanners. Calcification also blooms, and phase imaging distinguishes it from haemorrhage. Finally, do not count microbleeds within or immediately around the acute haematoma \u2014 they are part of the index bleed.",

changes.before: "detail": "Angiography, chemoembolisation, uterine fibroid embolisation and venous intervention are moderate risk \u2014 INR routinely, target INR < 1.5, aPTT < 1.5 \u00d7 control, platelets \u2265 50,000/\u03bcL. TIPS, biliary intervention through a new tract, complex ablation, renal biopsy and nephrostomy are high risk, and need INR, aPTT, platelets and haematocrit."

changes.before: "explain": "Conversion from red to yellow marrow runs from the periphery inwards and from distal to proximal within a limb, with epiphyses and apophyses turning fatty within months of their ossification centre appearing; the adult pattern \u2014 red marrow confined to the axial skeleton and the proximal femoral and humeral metaphyses \u2014 is settled by the mid-twenties. Reconversion simply runs the film backwards: axial skeleton first, then proximal to distal, and it spares epiphyses. Its drivers are smoking, obesity, altitude, chronic anaemia, endurance training and marrow-stimulating drugs, and this patient has two of them. The rules that protect you are on the T1 image: normal red marrow is brighter than muscle and than a normal disc, is symmetric and ill-defined, and does not touch cortex. Signal at or below muscle, epiphyseal involvement, or a focal well-defined lesion moves you the other way.",

changes.before: "explain": "Marrow oedema is a sign, not a diagnosis, and it is the company it keeps that tells you which one. Here the oedema is diffuse and undemarcated, crossing from head into neck without a boundary, and the subchondral bone is clean \u2014 the picture of transient osteoporosis of the hip, or bone marrow oedema syndrome, which affects middle-aged men and women in late pregnancy and settles over six to twelve months with protected loading. Avascular necrosis is defined by its border: a geographic serpiginous low-signal line on T1 and the double line on T2, with oedema appearing late as pain and collapse approach. A subchondral insufficiency fracture shows a low-signal line running parallel to and abutting the subchondral plate. Sepsis is worth a thought with an effusion, but that decision is driven by fever and inflammatory markers, and if they are up you aspirate regardless of the marrow pattern.",

A subchondral insufficiency fracture shows a low-signal line running parallel to and abutting the subchondral plate. changes.before: "explain": "The Fredericson scale escalates with what the marrow does: grade 1 is periosteal oedema with normal marrow, grade 2 adds marrow oedema seen only on fluid-sensitive sequences, grade 3 is marrow oedema also visible as low signal on T1, and grade 4 is a visible fracture line \u2014 commonly subdivided into 4a, intracortical signal, and 4b, a discrete line. Higher grades take longer to return to running, which is the grading's real use. But the site outranks the grade. This injury is on the posteromedial cortex, the compression side, and it heals with load modification. The same grade on the anterior cortex, which is loaded in tension, is a high-risk lesion prone to non-union. Report the grade if the referrer uses it, but report the surface without fail.",

Higher grades take longer to return to running, which is the grading's real use. But the site outranks the grade. changes.before: "explain": "The anterior tibial cortex is loaded in tension, and a stress fracture there tends not to heal: the lucency persists for months, may go on to complete fracture across the bone, and often needs intramedullary nailing rather than rest. That is what earns it high-risk status. The wider list of tension-side or poorly vascularised sites is worth carrying: the superolateral femoral neck, the medial malleolus, the tarsal navicular, the base of the fifth metatarsal at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction, the great toe sesamoids, the patella and the talus. Low-risk sites \u2014 posteromedial tibia, fibula, calcaneus, metatarsal shafts, femoral shaft, the compression side of the femoral neck \u2014 heal with rest. Osteoid osteoma is a fair differential, since it too thickens cortex, but its nidus is round and centred rather than a transverse line, and CT settles it.",

changes.before: "explain": "In the first fortnight there is a cellular, oedematous, enhancing mass with extensive surrounding oedema, and it can look exactly like a sarcoma on MRI \u2014 which is the whole danger of this lesion, because the early histology mimics sarcoma too, and an ill-timed biopsy has cost patients limbs. At around three to six weeks faint peripheral floccular calcification appears, and this zonal pattern is the diagnostic key: mature at the rim, immature in the centre, the reverse of an extraskeletal osteosarcoma, which mineralises most densely centrally and is most aggressive at its edge. Over a few months the rim corticates and a lucent cleft usually separates it from adjacent bone, and thereafter it commonly shrinks. The practical rule: when the appearance is early and worrying, repeat radiographs or CT in a few weeks rather than reaching for a needle. CT shows the rim before MRI does.",

changes.before: "explain": "Denervation oedema respects a nerve territory rather than a compartment or a vascular territory, and that is what makes it recognisable. Isolated infraspinatus signal places the lesion distal to the branch supplying supraspinatus, at the spinoglenoid notch, where a paralabral cyst is the usual culprit \u2014 and the cyst is usually fed by a posterior labral tear through a one-way valve. That tear is the finding that changes the operation, so search for it deliberately. A lesion at the suprascapular notch, higher up, would denervate supraspinatus as well. Teres minor with or without deltoid is the axillary nerve and the quadrilateral space. Multiple territories that fit no single nerve suggest Parsonage-Turner syndrome. Timing matters as much as location: acute denervation keeps normal bulk and normal T1, whereas chronic disease brings fatty T1 signal and volume loss, which does not reverse.",

changes.before: "explain": "Almost every painful diabetic forefoot lights up on STIR, so a report built on fluid-sensitive images alone will over-call infection and cost patients bone. The T1 image is the discriminator because osteomyelitis physically replaces marrow fat, and replacement is confluent and geographic rather than hazy and subcortical. Anatomy helps too: infection reaches bone by contiguous spread from the skin, so it sits directly beneath an ulcer at a pressure point \u2014 metatarsal heads, malleoli, the calcaneus \u2014 and a tract or a rim-enhancing collection joining ulcer to bone effectively closes the case. Two refinements. Post-contrast fat-suppressed sequences are for tracts and abscesses, not for making the marrow diagnosis. And say which bones are involved and how far the marrow signal extends, because that determines the level of resection.",
changes.after: "explain": "Almost every painful diabetic forefoot lights up on STIR, so a report built on fluid-sensitive images alone will over-call infection and cost patients bone. The T1 image is the discriminator because osteomyelitis physically replaces marrow fat, and replacement is confluent and geographic rather than hazy and subcortical. Anatomy helps too: infection reaches bone by contiguous spread from the skin, so it sits directly beneath an ulcer at a pressure point — metatarsal heads, malleoli, the calcaneus — and a tract or a rim-enhancing collection joining ulcer to bone effectively closes the case. Two refinements. Post-contrast fat-suppressed sequences are for tracts and abscesses, not for making the marrow diagnosis. And say which bones are involved and how far the marrow signal extends, because that determines the level of resection.",

changes.before: "explain": "Distribution normally separates the two conditions. Neuropathic arthropathy is a midfoot, periarticular disease \u2014 tarsometatarsal and naviculocuneiform subluxation, subchondral cysts, fragmentation, debris and deformity \u2014 while osteomyelitis is medullary and lies beneath an ulcer at a pressure point. The difficulty is that a rocker-bottom deformity manufactures a new pressure point, an ulcer forms over it, and the two then coexist, which is the situation described. The ghost sign is the useful pointer in that setting: a bone whose margins disappear on T1 within the surrounding oedema and then reappear after contrast or on T2 indicates infection rather than the ill-defined T1 loss of neuropathic marrow change. The tract from ulcer to cortex seals it. Name the infected bones explicitly, because that, not the diagnosis alone, is what the surgeon operates on.",

changes.before: "explain": "The lateral retropharyngeal nodes sit between the prevertebral muscles and the pharyngeal wall, above the hyoid, and they are the first echelon for the nasopharynx, the posterior pharyngeal wall and the sinonasal cavities. In adults they are ordinarily involuted and invisible, which is why the threshold is so much lower than in the neck proper: 5 mm short axis is the figure in common use, and some readers reserve a confident call for 8 mm or a node with necrosis. Children are different \u2014 reactive retropharyngeal nodes are a normal finding. The reason to hunt for these nodes is that a standard neck dissection does not reach them, so they are covered by the radiotherapy volume rather than by the surgeon. In the AJCC 8th edition staging of nasopharyngeal carcinoma, retropharyngeal nodal involvement counts within N1, so calling it changes the stage as well as the plan.",

changes.before: "explain": "The 8th edition, which is the edition head and neck staging still runs on, brought extranodal extension into the N category for the first time. For a p16-negative tumour, clinically overt extranodal extension makes the neck N3b whatever the size or number of nodes, so a 2.5 cm node that would otherwise be N1 leaps to the top of the N ladder. That is not bureaucracy: extranodal extension roughly halves survival, and its presence on the specimen is one of the two classic indications, with a positive margin, for concurrent chemotherapy alongside post-operative radiotherapy. Two cautions. Pathological staging is graded differently \u2014 a single ipsilateral node of 3 cm or less with extranodal extension is pN2a \u2014 and for p16-positive oropharyngeal cancer extranodal extension is deliberately excluded from the clinical N categories. On imaging, reserve the call for unequivocal signs: matted nodes and irradiated fat both mimic it.",

changes.before: "explain": "The level of the node is a map of where to look. The left supraclavicular fossa receives the thoracic duct, so a node there commonly reflects an infraclavicular primary \u2014 lung, oesophagus, stomach, pancreas, colon, kidney, ovary, testis or breast \u2014 and the appropriate next test is a CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis, often followed by PET-CT. The other options each describe a real pattern that does not fit this case. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma announces itself with retropharyngeal nodes and level V disease, usually in a younger patient, and the neck CT would rarely be clean. An HPV-associated oropharyngeal primary drains to a cystic level II node, not to the supraclavicular fossa. Thyroid carcinoma spreads to levels VI, III and IV and would be sought on ultrasound of a gland that is here normal. Learning the drainage territories is what turns an unexpected level from a curiosity into a direction of travel.",

changes.before: "explain": "Fine-needle aspiration is superb where the question is whether malignant epithelial cells are present \u2014 squamous carcinoma in a neck node, a thyroid nodule \u2014 because a cytological diagnosis needs only the cells. Lymphoma is diagnosed on how the cells are arranged as well as on what they are, and it is subclassified with immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry on tissue, so an aspirate yields the unhelpful answer this patient received. A core biopsy under ultrasound usually suffices and is the sensible next step; excisional biopsy of a whole node remains the reference standard when cores are equivocal. Note that the general warning against open biopsy of a neck node applies to suspected squamous carcinoma, not to suspected lymphoma, where excision is the right operation. When sampling, choose the node with the most abnormal cortex and vascularity rather than the largest, and avoid a node that is largely necrotic.",

changes.before: "explain": "The three phases answer three different questions. Flow and blood pool reflect regional hyperaemia and extracellular tracer, so cellulitis lights both; only osteomyelitis adds focal bone uptake on the delayed images, where soft tissue has cleared and the diphosphonate is bound to bone. A stress fracture is positive on all three phases early, with a focal delayed abnormality that is the whole point of the study. The genuinely difficult case is the neuropathic Charcot foot, which is hyperaemic and osteoblastically busy and so is positive on all phases too \u2014 which is why a bone scan alone cannot separate Charcot from superimposed osteomyelitis, and labelled white cell imaging with SPECT/CT, or MRI, is used instead. A negative delayed phase, as here, is the reassuring result: sensitivity for osteomyelitis is high, so its absence carries weight.",

changes.before: "explain": "A superscan is defined by the ratio, not the absolute counts: bone-to-soft-tissue contrast is so high that the kidneys become faint or invisible, the so-called absent kidney sign, because almost all the tracer has been extracted by bone. Its two families look subtly different. Diffuse osteoblastic metastasis, typically prostate or breast, is usually axial-predominant and slightly irregular on close inspection, with ribs and skull patchy. Metabolic bone disease \u2014 renal osteodystrophy, primary hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, myelofibrosis \u2014 gives a smoother pattern with prominent calvarium, mandible and costochondral junctions. Free pertechnetate from a poor radiolabel does the opposite: thyroid, salivary glands and stomach light up and the skeleton is faint. The trap this item guards against is dismissing a superscan as a beautiful normal study.",

changes.before: "explain": "The flare phenomenon is osteoblastic healing misread as disease. Lesions that are responding lay down new bone, which is exactly what a diphosphonate tracer measures, so uptake at known sites intensifies and deposits that were previously lytic and photopenic become visible for the first time. It appears roughly two to three months after starting effective therapy and settles thereafter. The discriminator is discordance: the images look worse while the patient and the biochemistry look better. Repeat imaging at around three to six months resolves it \u2014 genuine progression keeps progressing, flare fades. The same trap appears on radiographs, where lytic deposits becoming sclerotic is healing, and on PSMA imaging early after starting treatment. Calling flare progression costs the patient a drug that is working.",

changes.before: "explain": "A solitary hot spot in a patient with cancer is benign roughly half the time, so the planar image alone leaves you stranded. What SPECT/CT adds is precisely this: anatomical localisation within the vertebra, plus attenuation correction and better lesion contrast. Location decides the report. Uptake in a pedicle or in the vertebral body away from the endplate favours metastasis; uptake centred on a facet joint, an endplate with a Schmorl node, or an osteophyte is degenerative; a pars defect sits in the posterior elements, not the body. Ribs follow the same logic \u2014 several foci aligned in a vertical row are almost always traumatic. Correlating with the CT component turns an equivocal study into a definite answer and spares the patient an MRI, a delay and an anxious week.",

changes.before: "explain": "Mismatch is the diagnostic unit: a perfusion defect with preserved ventilation, segmental or subsegmental in shape, wedge-shaped and pleural-based. Two such defects are convincing evidence of embolism. The left base here is a triple match \u2014 perfusion defect, ventilation defect and radiographic opacity \u2014 which is not evidence of embolus, since pneumonia, atelectasis and infarct all produce it; conventionally it is reported as indeterminate for that region, particularly in the lower zones. Crucially, an indeterminate region does not contaminate an unequivocal mismatch elsewhere; you report both, and the patient is anticoagulated. Modern practice, especially with V/Q SPECT, has moved away from PIOPED probability language towards a three-way report of embolism present, absent, or study non-diagnostic.",

Modern practice, especially with V/Q SPECT, has moved away from PIOPED probability language towards a three-way report of embolism present, absent, or study non-diagnostic.",

changes.before: "explain": "The thyroid scan separates the two mechanisms of thyrotoxicosis, and the treatments diverge completely. Overproduction shows increased uptake: Graves disease diffusely and homogeneously, a toxic adenoma as one hot nodule with the remaining gland suppressed, a toxic multinodular goitre as patchy areas of activity. Destruction shows low or absent uptake, because preformed hormone is leaking from a gland that is not making any \u2014 subacute de Quervain thyroiditis, silent and postpartum thyroiditis, amiodarone type 2, and exogenous thyroxine. Antithyroid drugs and radioiodine work in the first group and are useless in the second, which needs analgesia, sometimes steroids, and time. Separately, in a euthyroid patient with a nodule, a hot nodule is almost never malignant and does not need aspiration, while a cold nodule is assessed on ultrasound and aspirated on its sonographic features.",

changes.before: "explain": "Hepatobiliary agents are extracted by hepatocytes and excreted into bile along the same pathway as bilirubin, so the study is a map of bile flow. Duodenal activity proves the common duct is patent, which excludes distal obstruction. Non-visualisation of the gallbladder in that setting means the cystic duct is blocked, and cystic duct obstruction is the functional definition of acute cholecystitis. changes.before: "explain": "O-RADS US 1 is the normal premenopausal ovary, and it includes a follicle up to 3 cm and a corpus luteum up to 3 cm. These are physiology, not findings; describing them, following them and measuring them generates anxiety and repeat scans for nothing. Above 3 cm and up to 10 cm a simple cyst becomes O-RADS 2 \u2014 almost certainly benign, under 1% risk \u2014 and even then most need no imaging follow-up. The postmenopausal ovary is different: category 1 does not apply to it, because it should not be making follicles, so a simple cyst there is scored 2 rather than 1. Even so, the Society of Radiologists in Ultrasound consensus regards a simple cyst of 1 cm or less in a postmenopausal woman as clinically inconsequential and not worth describing. Knowing what to leave out is part of the skill.",

changes.before: "explain": "Morphology alone would keep this in O-RADS 2: a simple cyst has anechoic contents, a smooth thin wall and posterior acoustic enhancement, and there is no solid tissue anywhere. But O-RADS US applies a size rule on top of morphology. A simple cyst above 3 cm and below 10 cm is category 2, almost certainly benign. At 10 cm or more it becomes category 3 \u2014 low risk, in the 1% to under 10% band \u2014 because very large cysts carry a small but real chance of a cystadenoma or a borderline tumour, and because their size itself raises the risk of torsion or rupture. The same 10 cm rule pushes the other classic benign lesions, such as a haemorrhagic cyst, an endometrioma or a dermoid, from category 2 into category 3. The practical consequence is that this woman needs gynaecological assessment, with MRI or specialist ultrasound as an option, not simple discharge.",

changes.before: "explain": "The O-RADS US colour score comes from the IOTA lexicon: 1 is no flow, 2 minimal, 3 moderate and 4 very strong. For a multilocular cyst with no solid tissue, the category depends on three things \u2014 size, the smoothness of the inner wall, and the colour score. Smooth, under 10 cm, colour score 1 to 3 gives category 3. Reaching 10 cm, or having an irregular inner wall, or a colour score of 4, moves it to category 4, the 10% to under 50% band. Colour score 4 does not by itself produce a category 5; that requires solid tissue behaviour, four or more papillary projections, an irregular solid lesion, or ascites with peritoneal nodularity. Category 4 is the band where MRI earns its place, because most category 4 lesions are reclassified downwards once the tissue is characterised.",

changes.before: "explain": "A papillary projection in the O-RADS lexicon is solid tissue at least 3 mm high protruding into the cyst lumen, and it is counted whether or not it shows flow \u2014 vascularity raises suspicion but is not required for it to count. The number is what moves the category: a cystic lesion with one to three projections is O-RADS 4, and four or more takes it to O-RADS 5, the band at 50% risk or above. Other routes into category 5 are a solid lesion with an irregular outer contour and any colour score, a smooth solid lesion with colour score 4, and the presence of ascites with peritoneal nodules regardless of the lesion itself. Category 5 means the referral is to gynaecological oncology, because outcomes in ovarian cancer depend heavily on who performs the primary surgery.",

changes.before: "explain": "The purpose of O-RADS MRI is to rescue lesions from the indeterminate middle. Ultrasound can see that there is solid tissue but often cannot say what kind, and the intermediate-risk band spans 10% to just under 50% \u2014 too high to ignore and too low to justify oncological surgery. MRI answers the tissue question three ways: fat suppression identifies a dermoid, uniformly dark tissue on T2 and on high b-value diffusion identifies benign fibrous tissue, and dynamic contrast gives a time-intensity curve that separates low, intermediate and high risk. In practice a large share of O-RADS US 4 lesions come down to MRI 2 or 3. What MRI cannot do is add value when the diagnosis is already made: ascites with peritoneal nodularity is O-RADS 5 on ultrasound alone, and the delay of a further scan costs the patient time.",

changes.before: "explain": "O-RADS MRI uses the outer myometrium as an internal reference standard, which neatly removes the effect of injection rate and cardiac output. Three curve types are recognised. The low-risk curve rises gradually without an early shoulder and stays below the myometrium; it gives a score of 3, roughly a 5% risk. The intermediate curve has a shoulder and then a plateau but enhances later and less than the myometrium; that is a score of 4, around 50%. The high-risk curve enhances earlier than the myometrium and plateaus above it, reflecting neovascular shunting; that is a score of 5, around 90%. If dynamic imaging is unavailable, the fallback is a single comparison with the outer myometrium at 30 to 40 seconds. Note that the curve is only needed for solid tissue that is not uniformly dark on T2 and diffusion \u2014 that tissue is already benign.",

changes.before: "explain": "The haemorrhagic cyst is the commonest cause of an anxious adnexal report, and it has a reliable signature. Early on, fibrin strands make a fine reticular or fishnet pattern with no flow. As the clot organises it retracts from the wall, producing a solid-looking element that is nonetheless avascular and has straight or concave margins where it has pulled away \u2014 the opposite of the convex bulging outline of a true papillary projection. Nothing inside a haemorrhagic cyst should show Doppler flow, although flow in the surrounding ovarian tissue is normal. The lesion evolves and disappears, usually within about eight weeks, which is why the classic safety net is a repeat scan in the six to twelve week window, timed just after a period. On MRI it is bright on T1 and on fat-suppressed T1, variable on T2, and it does not enhance.",

changes.before: "explain": "Two signal facts do the work here. Staying bright on fat-suppressed T1 means the content is blood, not fat \u2014 a dermoid loses its signal the moment fat saturation is applied. Losing signal on T2 is shading, caused by chronically degraded blood products with high protein and iron concentration, and it is characteristic of the endometrioma rather than the acute haemorrhagic cyst. The very dark dependent focus, the T2 dark spot, is more specific still. That combination is O-RADS MRI 2, almost certainly benign. Two things belong in the report nonetheless. First, endometriomas travel with deep infiltrating disease, so the uterosacral ligaments, torus, rectovaginal septum and bowel deserve a look. Second, malignant transformation, although uncommon, is announced by an enhancing mural nodule, loss of the usual shading, or interval growth, most often in women over 45.",

changes.before: "explain": "The commonest error in suspected torsion is trusting the Doppler. The ovary has a dual arterial supply, from the ovarian artery and from the ovarian branch of the uterine artery, and torsion is often intermittent or incomplete, so arterial flow may persist in an ovary that is nonetheless twisted and dying. Venous and lymphatic drainage fails first, which is exactly why the grey-scale findings \u2014 a unilaterally enlarged oedematous ovary, follicles pushed to the periphery by stromal oedema, a whirlpool of twisted vessels at the pedicle, the ovary sitting in an abnormal midline or superior position, and free fluid \u2014 carry more weight than the colour box. In adults a lead mass is usually present, most often a dermoid. Torsion is a surgical emergency in which detorsion salvages ovarian function, so the report should escalate rather than defer to further imaging.",

changes.before: "explain": "Stage III of the FIGO system is subdivided by how much extrapelvic peritoneal disease there is. IIIA1 is retroperitoneal nodal disease alone, further split by whether the largest node is at or below 10 mm. IIIA2 is microscopic extrapelvic peritoneal involvement. IIIB is macroscopic extrapelvic peritoneal deposits measuring 2 cm or less, and IIIC is deposits larger than 2 cm \u2014 a category that also captures tumour on the capsule of the liver or spleen without invasion of the parenchyma. That capsule-versus-parenchyma distinction is the one radiologists are asked to make most often, because parenchymal liver metastasis is stage IVB. Stage IVA is a malignant pleural effusion with positive cytology, and IVB covers parenchymal metastases, transmural bowel involvement and disease outside the abdomen, including inguinal nodes. Measure the largest deposit, and say plainly whether liver disease is on the surface or within it.",

changes.before: "explain": "Two intramural findings and one vascular one. Gas within the bowel wall is pneumatosis, bubbly where it is submucosal and curvilinear where it dissects subserosally, and in a preterm infant of this age with these symptoms it is diagnostic of necrotising enterocolitis. The branching lucencies over the liver are portal venous gas, and the direction of flow tells them apart from gas in the biliary tree: portal blood flows towards the periphery, so portal gas reaches within a couple of centimetres of the capsule, while bile drains centrally, so biliary gas sits around the hilum. Portal gas marks more extensive disease \u2014 stage IIB in the modified Bell system \u2014 and predicts a worse course, but it is not by itself a reason to operate. Free intraperitoneal gas is. So the plan is medical: stop feeds, decompress the stomach, antibiotics, cultures, and frequent films while the child is unstable, with ultrasound adding wall thickness, wall perfusion, free fluid and bubbles seen moving in the portal vein.",

changes.before: "explain": "The value of serial films is comparison rather than any single appearance. Normal bowel is restless; a loop that holds its shape and position through several films has stopped moving, and a segment that has stopped moving is usually ischaemic. Persistent asymmetric dilatation and increasing separation of loops by fluid carry the same warning. Pneumoperitoneum remains the one agreed absolute indication for surgery in necrotising enterocolitis, and it is easy to miss on a supine film in a distended abdomen \u2014 look also for Rigler's sign, where both sides of the bowel wall are outlined, for the falciform ligament drawn as a line, and for a triangle of gas between loops. The left lateral decubitus is preferred over an erect film because a sick preterm infant tolerates the position and the liver gives a reliable background; a cross-table lateral with the infant left supine is the fallback when turning is impossible.",

changes.before: "explain": "Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with midgut volvulus until a study says otherwise, and the reason for the urgency is anatomical: a narrow mesenteric base lets the whole midgut twist about the superior mesenteric vessels, and once it does, the entire small bowel can infarct within hours. The plain film is the trap here, because in early volvulus it is commonly normal or nearly so \u2014 a soft abdomen and some distal gas exclude nothing. The upper gastrointestinal series remains the reference standard because it shows the position of the duodenojejunal flexure directly. Ultrasound is a useful adjunct and can show the whirlpool of the mesenteric vein wrapping the artery, but a normal vein-to-artery relationship does not exclude malrotation and an abnormal one does not prove volvulus. The enema is unreliable, since a mobile caecum is common in normal neonates and a normally sited caecum does not exclude a narrow mesentery. Waiting six hours is the one option that can cost the bowel.",

changes.before: "explain": "Two coordinates define the flexure and both must be satisfied: left of the left-sided pedicle, and as high as the bulb. The commonest cause of a wrong answer is not anatomy but positioning, because any rotation of the infant swings the duodenum across the spine and manufactures both false positives and false negatives \u2014 so check that the film is truly frontal before calling anything abnormal, and repeat it if it is not. Technique matters as much: give a small volume of contrast and watch the first swallow under fluoroscopy, because once the stomach is full it overlies and hides the duodenum. A lateral run then confirms that the third part passes posteriorly and retroperitoneally as it should. The corkscrew and the beak are the signs of an established twist, and they turn an urgent study into an immediate call to theatre for a Ladd procedure.",

changes.before: "explain": "The study is a piece of real-time observation rather than a set of pictures, and the sequence is the study. Contrast passes the oesophagus, fills the stomach, enters the cap, descends as the second part along the right of the spine, crosses the midline behind the stomach as the third part, and rises to the flexure on the left. Everything hinges on that last transition, so the first swallow is the important one \u2014 after that, contrast pooled in the stomach projects over the duodenum and obscures exactly what you came to see. Practical consequences follow: use a small volume, have the infant supine and square to the table, and be ready to turn to a lateral immediately afterwards to confirm the retroperitoneal course of the third part. If the flexure cannot be seen because of overlying stomach, the honest report says the study was not diagnostic and repeats it, rather than reassuring a surgeon about a landmark nobody saw.",

changes.before: "explain": "The two bubbles say the obstruction is duodenal; the distal gas says it is incomplete, and that changes everything. Complete duodenal atresia gives a double bubble with a gasless abdomen beyond it, and it can wait for a planned operation after the infant is resuscitated. Gas distal to the block means the lumen is still partly open \u2014 a stenosis, a fenestrated web, an annular pancreas \u2014 or, and this is the possibility that cannot wait, malrotation with midgut volvulus obstructing the third part. So the presence of distal gas converts an elective operation into an urgent contrast study to site the duodenojejunal flexure. Trisomy 21 accompanies roughly a third of duodenal atresias and makes atresia more likely, but it confers no protection against volvulus. A more distal atresia, such as jejunal, gives three or four dilated loops with levels and no gas beyond; Hirschsprung disease obstructs at the other end of the bowel; and pyloric stenosis gives non-bilious vomiting at several weeks with a single bubble.",

changes.before: "explain": "Pylorospasm is the great imitator, and time is what separates it from hypertrophy. The cut-offs in common use are a single-wall muscle thickness of 3 mm or more and a channel length of about 15 to 17 mm or more, with thickness the more reliable of the two \u2014 and these measurements fall below both. More telling than any number is behaviour: a spastic pylorus eventually relaxes and lets fluid through, whereas a hypertrophied one does not open however long you watch. Technique protects you from both errors. Use a high-frequency linear probe, turn the infant into a right posterior oblique so gastric fluid falls into the antrum and outlines the channel, find the true long axis, and measure the anterior muscle wall perpendicular to it, since an obliquely cut or contracted antrum manufactures thickness. If the infant is the right age with the right history and the numbers sit just under the threshold, the correct report asks for a repeat scan in a day or two rather than declaring the study normal.",

changes.before: "explain": "This is the point where imaging hands over to physiology. Losing gastric contents means losing hydrogen ions and chloride; the kidney defends volume by retaining sodium and, running short of chloride, excretes potassium and hydrogen in exchange, which deepens the alkalosis and produces the paradoxical aciduria of a late presentation. An infant in that state is dehydrated and hypoventilating to compensate, and general anaesthesia on top of it is associated with apnoea in recovery. Pyloromyotomy relieves an obstruction that has been building for weeks; a few more hours of correction cost nothing and remove the main anaesthetic risk. Saying this in the report \u2014 or on the phone \u2014 is part of the radiologist's job, because the enthusiasm to operate on a confirmed diagnosis is exactly what the finding tends to generate.",

changes.before: "explain": "Measure the doughnut, because size decides what it is and what you do. An ileocolic intussusception is bulky, typically well over 2.5 cm in diameter, sits under the right ribs or across the upper abdomen, persists while you watch, and needs treatment. A small-bowel intussusception is small, usually under 2 cm, short, central, transient, and is left alone \u2014 the layered target and the pseudokidney look identical, so the diameter and the location do the work. Trapped peritoneal fluid between the layers, absent Doppler flow in the walls and a long history all predict a harder reduction and a higher chance of needing surgery, but none of them forbids an attempt. Preparation is the substance of the answer: intravenous access, a resuscitated child, an informed surgical team, and the enema done in the department by someone who does them. CT contributes nothing before the attempt, and a lead point is uncommon below the age of two.",

changes.before: "explain": "Gas drawn along the falciform ligament on a supine film is free intraperitoneal gas, and free gas means the bowel is already open. Insufflating a perforated colon pushes air into the peritoneum under pressure and can produce a tension pneumoperitoneum that splints the diaphragm and obstructs venous return within seconds. Perforation, peritonitis and haemodynamic instability are the accepted contraindications to attempted reduction, and this child has all three; a lower pressure does not make an open bowel safe, and hydrostatic reduction has the same objection. By contrast, a long history, small-bowel obstruction, a known lead point and the extremes of age are relative factors: they lower the success rate and shape the conversation with the surgeon, but they do not forbid an attempt in a stable child. The enema is never the resuscitation \u2014 fluid, analgesia and a surgical team come first in every case, and here they come instead.",

changes.before: "explain": "The wording of the conclusion is the clinical act here. Ultrasound is the right first test in a child \u2014 no radiation, no sedation, and a positive study is a positive study: a blind-ending non-compressible tube over 6 mm in diameter, often with an appendicolith, surrounding echogenic inflamed fat, hyperaemia and free fluid. Its weakness is negative work. Visualisation rates vary with body habitus, bowel gas and operator, and the appendix hiding behind the caecum or down in the pelvis is precisely the one that fails to appear. If a report of that study reads 'normal appendix not seen \u2014 no appendicitis', a surgeon may be reassured about a child who has it. Say instead that the appendix was not visualised, list the secondary signs that were absent, and set out the two acceptable paths, so that the decision returns to the clinical assessment where it belongs.",

changes.before: "explain": "Five hours have gone, so one remains \u2014 which is the whole argument for arranging the scan around the operation rather than in front of it. Where the history and examination are convincing, sudden pain with a high-riding transverse testis and an absent cremasteric reflex, the boy goes to theatre and imaging must not delay him; a normal scan does not overrule that picture. When ultrasound is done, compare with the normal side, turn the Doppler settings right down for slow flow, and look for two things: reduced or absent intratesticular flow, and the twisted cord above the testis, seen as a whirlpool of vessels. The cord sign is the more specific, and it is the one that still holds when torsion is incomplete and some arterial flow persists. A focal tender nodule at the upper pole with preserved testicular flow is torsion of an appendix testis, which is treated with analgesia and does not need an operation.",

changes.before: "explain": "Two things carry this: the gestation and the volumes. Surfactant is made by type II pneumocytes from about 24 weeks and is not reliably adequate until around 34, so a 27-week lung collapses at end expiration. That microatelectasis is what the fine granularity is, and the underinflated lung \u2014 six posterior ribs on a ventilated baby is low \u2014 is the discriminator, because retained fetal lung fluid and meconium aspiration both give normal or increased volumes. Retained fluid is a term or near-term problem, streaky rather than granular, with fluid in a fissure. Meconium gives coarse, asymmetric, rope-like opacity in a post-term baby. Group B streptococcal pneumonia is the true mimic, since it can reproduce a granular lung exactly, but it does so in a term infant and more often carries an effusion. Expect the appearance to change within hours of surfactant, often asymmetrically as some segments recruit before others, and then watch for the air leak that a newly compliant lung on unchanged pressures invites.",

changes.before: "explain": "This is retained fetal lung fluid. Labour and the passage through the birth canal clear the fetal lung; an elective caesarean skips both, so the fluid leaves slowly by the lymphatics and the interstitium stays wet. That gives exactly what is described \u2014 normal to increased volumes, perihilar streaks, fluid tracking into a fissure, sometimes a small effusion \u2014 and it settles as the lymphatics catch up, typically inside a day or two. The imaging decision is to do nothing more. Surfactant deficiency would show low volumes and granularity, not fissural fluid, and giving surfactant to a wet lung treats the wrong problem. The effusion here is transudative and tiny; tapping it is a needle for no information. A clinical sepsis screen may well be started in any tachypnoeic newborn, and that is reasonable, but nothing on this film argues for pneumonia or for a 24-hour film to chase it. If the tachypnoea has not settled by 48 hours, that is the moment to think again.",

changes.before: "explain": "Meconium is a particulate obstruction, not a compliance problem. Plugs lodge in bronchi and act as ball valves, so gas enters on inspiration and cannot leave: the lung overinflates, the diaphragms flatten and the chest looks barrel-shaped on the lateral. Around the plugs there is patchy atelectasis and chemical pneumonitis, which is why the shadowing is coarse and asymmetric \u2014 one lobe is dense, the next is over-aerated. Surfactant deficiency does the opposite: it is a uniform disease of a uniformly immature lung, and the lung is small. That combination of trapped gas, uneven compliance and a ventilator makes air leak common in meconium aspiration \u2014 a fifth to a third of ventilated cases \u2014 so every film is read first for a deep sulcus, a hyperlucent hemithorax or a thymus lifted off the heart. Small pleural effusions also occur, and secondary surfactant inactivation means some of these babies do receive surfactant.",

changes.before: "explain": "Interstitial gas comes from alveolar rupture into the perivascular sheaths, and once there it cannot be exhaled. That is why the lucencies are fixed between inspiration and expiration and why the lung stays expanded and stiff \u2014 the tell that separates them from air bronchograms, which branch, taper and change. It also explains the mass effect: a lung splinted open by gas in its own interstitium compresses its neighbour and impedes venous return. Pleural air would collect at a surface and shift with position, and there are no lung markings within a pneumothorax. A congenital malformation is present from birth, not on day five. The management is to take the pressure out of the system \u2014 lower peak and mean airway pressure, accept a higher carbon dioxide, consider high-frequency oscillation \u2014 and to use gravity, nursing the affected side dependent so that lung is less well ventilated and can decompress. Interstitial emphysema is a warning shot: pneumothorax and pneumomediastinum follow it.",

changes.before: "explain": "Mediastinal gas has a characteristic geography because it is confined by fascial planes. It rises between the thymic lobes and lifts them off the heart, giving the sail-like appearance sometimes drawn as an angel's wing, and it tracks under the heart so that the two hemidiaphragms appear joined by a continuous lucent line \u2014 an appearance a pneumothorax cannot produce, because pleural air stops at the mediastinal reflection. The decubitus film is the honest test of any equivocal lucency in a baby: pleural air is free and obeys gravity, mediastinal air is trapped and does not. Treatment is usually nothing. Mediastinal air decompresses along the fascial planes into the neck or the retroperitoneum, and it does not tamponade the way pleural air does unless the volume is large. What it does mean is that alveolar rupture has occurred, so the ventilator settings deserve review and every later film is read for the pneumothorax that may follow.",

It exerts no mass effect \u2014 the trachea stays midline and no vessel or bronchus is displaced \u2014 and its margin is soft and deformable, indented by the ribs and blending with the mediastinum rather than sharply marginated. If doubt remained, ultrasound settles it without radiation, showing a homogeneous low-echogenicity structure with fine echogenic septa that changes shape with respiration.",

changes.before: "explain": "The catheter follows the fetal circulation in reverse. It enters the umbilical vein, meets the left branch of the portal vein, and is carried by the ductus venosus \u2014 the fetal shunt that bypasses the liver \u2014 into the inferior vena cava, coming to rest at the junction with the right atrium, which projects at about the eighth to ninth thoracic vertebra, just above the diaphragm. That level matters. A tip that stops short and turns caudally has gone down the portal system, where hypertonic dextrose and drugs risk portal thrombosis and hepatic injury; a tip pushed deep into the atrium risks arrhythmia, and through the atrial wall risks a pericardial effusion and tamponade. The arterial line is the mirror image: it descends into an internal iliac artery before turning up the aorta, and it is parked either high, between the sixth and ninth thoracic vertebrae, or low, between the third and fifth lumbar, deliberately avoiding the stretch from the tenth thoracic to the second lumbar vertebra where the coeliac, mesenteric and renal arteries arise.",

changes.before: "explain": "The size-specific dose estimate is simply the CTDIvol multiplied by a size conversion factor, so 4.0 times 1.9 gives 7.6 mGy. The point of the arithmetic is what CTDIvol is not: it is the scanner's output measured in a plastic cylinder, not the dose the child absorbed. A small child attenuates less and is closer in size to the beam, so the same output deposits more energy per gram \u2014 hence a factor above one, rising as the child gets smaller. AAPM Report 204 tabulates those factors against effective diameter, and Report 220 refines the input to water-equivalent diameter. Two cautions travel with the number. First, check which phantom the CTDIvol refers to: a body protocol reported on the 32 cm phantom gives a figure roughly half the same exposure expressed on the 16 cm phantom, so comparing scanners without checking the reference is meaningless. Second, the size-specific estimate is still not organ dose and still not effective dose.",

changes.before: "explain": "Dividing 1.4 by 0.02 gives 70. The exact ratio is not the lesson \u2014 it moves with the scanner, the protocol and the size of the child, and a well-optimised chest CT in an infant can be far lower than the figure used here \u2014 but the order of magnitude is, because it is what should govern the choice between repeating a film and adding a scan. A follow-up radiograph is close to free; a repeat CT is not, and a multiphase CT multiplies itself. Children matter more than adults for two independent reasons: dividing tissues are more radiosensitive, and a child has decades in which a stochastic effect can appear. The practical levers are all unglamorous \u2014 set the tube current to the child rather than to an adult default, drop the kilovoltage, remove the anti-scatter grid for small chests, collimate to the anatomy asked about, scan one phase, and ask first whether ultrasound or MRI answers the question at all.",

changes.before: "explain": "Nearly everything children inhale \u2014 food, plastic, nuts \u2014 is radiolucent, so you are not looking for the object but for what it does. A partially obstructing bronchial foreign body works as a ball valve: gas passes on inspiration and is trapped on expiration, so the affected lung stays inflated, is relatively lucent, and pushes the mediastinum away as the normal side empties. An expiratory film demonstrates this, but a toddler will not hold her breath out. The decubitus achieves the same thing with gravity: the dependent hemithorax should lose volume under the weight of the mediastinum and the abdominal contents, and a dependent lung that stays fully inflated is trapping. Filming both sides makes the child her own control. Two caveats decide management: a completely normal set does not exclude an inhaled foreign body, and where the history is as clear as this one, bronchoscopy is both the definitive test and the treatment. CT adds dose and delay; the swallow examines the wrong tube.",
changes.after: "explain": "Nearly everything children inhale — food, plastic, nuts — is radiolucent, so you are not looking for the object but for what it does. A partially obstructing bronchial foreign body works as a ball valve: gas passes on inspiration and is trapped on expiration, so the affected lung stays inflated, is relatively lucent, and pushes the mediastinum away as the normal side empties. An expiratory film demonstrates this, but a toddler will not hold her breath out. The decubitus achieves the same thing with gravity: the dependent hemithorax should lose volume under the weight of the mediastinum and the abdominal contents, and a dependent lung that stays fully inflated is trapping. Filming both sides makes the child her own control. Two caveats decide management: a completely normal set does not exclude an inhaled foreign body, and where the history is as clear as this one, bronchoscopy is both the definitive test and the treatment. CT adds dose and delay; the swallow examines the wrong tube.",

changes.before: "explain": "A round pneumonia is a consequence of immature anatomy. The collateral channels that let infection spread through an adult lung segment \u2014 the pores of Kohn and the canals of Lambert \u2014 develop through childhood, so in a young child the infection expands as a sphere from where it started, usually posteriorly and in a lower lobe, usually pneumococcal, usually solitary. The air bronchogram is the finding that keeps you honest: patent bronchi running through it means airspace disease, not a soft-tissue mass, which would displace or occlude them. So the correct action is to treat and to arrange a follow-up film once treated, conventionally at about four to six weeks, to confirm it has gone. That plan also protects the child who turns out to have something else, because a lesion that does not clear is precisely the one that earns cross-sectional imaging. Scanning or biopsying pneumonia at presentation exposes a child for a diagnosis the antibiotics were about to make, and there is no effusion here to hunt with ultrasound.",

changes.before: "explain": "Bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis, and this history \u2014 coryza then wheeze in an infant in winter \u2014 is the textbook one. None of that alters the treatment, which is oxygen, feeding support and time, but the collapse looks like consolidation to anyone reading quickly, and studies of routine radiography in bronchiolitis consistently find higher antibiotic prescribing without better outcomes. changes.before: "explain": "In the Graf method the baseline runs along the iliac wing, the bony roof line along the acetabular roof, and the angle between them is alpha. Alpha of 60 degrees or more is a mature hip \u2014 Graf type I \u2014 and a beta angle under 55 degrees puts it in subtype Ia. More than half the femoral head sitting under bony roof agrees. Breech presentation is a proper screening indication, and six weeks is the right moment: scanning in the first few weeks catches physiological laxity and generates false positives that lead to unnecessary harnesses. Repeat scanning belongs to the immature type IIa hip (alpha 50\u201359 degrees under three months), not to this one. Nothing here needs a harness, and a radiograph at six weeks is largely uninterpretable because the femoral head has not yet ossified.",

changes.before: "explain": "Sixty degrees is the line Graf drew between a mature hip and everything else, and it is worth holding on to because every other threshold in the system hangs off it. Alpha of 50\u201359 degrees is a deficient bony roof: type IIa if the infant is under three months (physiological immaturity, rescan), type IIb if over three months (true dysplasia, treat). Alpha of 43\u201349 degrees is a critical hip, subdivided by beta \u2014 type IIc if beta is under 77 degrees, type D if beta exceeds it, meaning the head is beginning to decentre. Below 43 degrees the hip is dislocated: type III with the labrum everted, type IV with it pressed down between head and roof. The alpha angle is only trustworthy on a correctly obtained coronal image with a straight iliac line, so judge the image before you trust the number.",

Below 43 degrees the hip is dislocated: type III with the labrum everted, type IV with it pressed down between head and roof. The alpha angle is only trustworthy on a correctly obtained coronal image with a straight iliac line, so judge the image before you trust the number.",

changes.before: "explain": "Two separate statements are being made here and they carry different weight. Position \u2014 epiphysis lateral and superior, Shenton's arc broken \u2014 tells you where the head is now, and it is out. The acetabular index tells you what the socket has become in response, and a steep roof at 38 degrees at fourteen months is well outside the normal range, which is falling towards 25 degrees by the first birthday. That matters for management: a hip that is simply lax may reduce and remodel, whereas a steep, shallow, false-acetabulum-forming socket in a walking child usually needs open reduction with a pelvic osteotomy rather than a harness, which in any case is ineffective beyond about six months. Say both things in the report, because the surgeon plans from the acetabulum, not only from the head.",

changes.before: "explain": "This is the early face of Perthes disease \u2014 idiopathic osteonecrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis, typically a boy of four to eight, insidious limp, pain often referred to the knee. The earliest reliable radiographic signs are a small dense nucleus, apparent medial joint space widening, and the subchondral fracture line, the crescent sign, which lies anterosuperiorly and is therefore hidden on the AP and shown on the frog-lateral. Finding it establishes the diagnosis and predicts the extent of the segment that will fragment. If both views stay normal and suspicion persists, contrast-enhanced or perfusion MRI shows the avascular segment weeks before the radiograph does. Inlet and outlet views belong to pelvic trauma. Waiting six months wastes the containment window, which is when treatment changes the outcome.",

changes.before: "explain": "The line of Klein along the superior femoral neck should clip a sliver of the lateral epiphysis on the AP; when it misses entirely, the epiphysis has slipped posteromedially, and that failure carries Trethowan's name. A widened, irregular physis with loss of epiphyseal height supports it. Two things then drive management. First, a stable slip becomes unstable if he keeps walking, and an unstable slip carries a high rate of avascular necrosis, so he stops weight-bearing at once and goes to the orthopaedic team today. Second, the contralateral hip slips in a substantial minority \u2014 figures of roughly 20 to 40 per cent are quoted \u2014 so it is imaged and watched. A frog-lateral or cross-table lateral is more sensitive for a subtle slip, but positioning a frankly unstable hip in frog is avoided. MRI is unnecessary when the radiograph is this clear.",

changes.before: "explain": "The commonest error here is treating a positive scan as a diagnosis. Capsular distension of more than about 2 mm, or 2 mm more than the other side, is a real effusion, and it is present in transient synovitis, in septic arthritis, in early Perthes and in juvenile idiopathic arthritis alike. Echogenicity of the fluid does not reliably separate pus from serous fluid. What the scan genuinely does is exclude an effusion when there is none, and guide the needle when there is one. changes.before: "explain": "The sequence is worth knowing cold because it is a safety check, not a piece of trivia. Capitellum, radial head, internal (medial) epicondyle, trochlea, olecranon, external (lateral) epicondyle, appearing at roughly one, three, five, seven, nine and eleven years, with wide individual variation and earlier appearance in girls. Ages are approximate; the order is not. Two practical consequences follow. First, an unfused centre in the expected sequence is never a fracture, so knowing the order stops you overcalling normality. Second, and more importantly, the medial epicondyle always ossifies before the trochlea, so a fragment at the trochlea with no medial epicondyle in place means the medial epicondyle has been avulsed \u2014 usually into the joint after a dislocation. changes.before: "explain": "Lateral condylar fractures are usually Salter\u2013Harris type IV, crossing metaphysis, physis and unossified epiphyseal cartilage into the joint, and the extensor origin pulls the fragment laterally and rotates it. The internal oblique projection profiles the fracture best and routinely shows more displacement than the AP, which is why it changes decisions: gapping beyond roughly 2 mm, or any widening on serial films, usually goes to fixation, while a genuinely undisplaced fracture may be casted with close review. Missing or under-treating one is expensive \u2014 non-union, cubitus valgus and a tardy ulnar nerve palsy years later. Where the cartilaginous hinge cannot be judged, ultrasound or MRI can be used acutely in some centres, but a delayed outpatient scan is no help. Ultrasound is diagnostic when the muscle is expanded but its contour and internal fibrillar pattern are maintained and there is no separate mass, no necrosis and no abnormal nodes. It resolves over months with stretching, and imaging or biopsy beyond the initial scan is unnecessary and can be misleading, since the histology is cellular and has been misread as sarcoma. The distinction between II and III is the ventricular size, which is why the measurement matters and why serial scans track it \u2014 post-haemorrhagic ventricular dilatation is the complication that leads to shunting. changes.before: "explain": "SUV is not a measurement of the tumour so much as a ratio: activity concentration in the region divided by injected activity per unit body weight. Everything in that chain travels badly between departments \u2014 uptake time, plasma glucose, any dose extravasation, scanner calibration, and reconstruction (point spread function and time-of-flight modelling both push small-lesion SUVmax up). Harmonisation programmes such as EARL exist precisely because raw numbers are not portable. Quantitative response assessment (PERCIST) therefore demands the same scanner, protocol and uptake time. RECIST 1.1 is an anatomical system; it uses FDG PET only in a limited way, to confirm that a new lesion is genuinely new, and it never grades response by SUV. A falling SUV would need a longer, not shorter, uptake time to be an artefact, since tumour uptake rises for the first hour or more.",

A falling SUV would need a longer, not shorter, uptake time to be an artefact, since tumour uptake rises for the first hour or more.",

changes.before: "explain": "Brown fat is metabolically active, sympathetically driven and richest in young, thin, female patients scanned in cold weather. Its signature is symmetry and distribution: supraclavicular and lower neck, paravertebral, perirenal, around the aortic arch and in the mediastinal fat, always with fat attenuation on the co-registered CT rather than a soft tissue node. That co-registration is the whole reason PET is fused with CT. The clinical problem is not misdiagnosis so much as concealment \u2014 brown fat sits exactly where supraclavicular and mediastinal nodes sit and can mask them. Prevention is practical: a warm waiting room and blankets, avoiding cold exposure before injection, and in some departments a benzodiazepine or a beta blocker. If the neck genuinely has to be assessed, rescan the patient warm rather than argue with the images you have.",

changes.before: "explain": "PET is far better than CT at finding mediastinal disease, but a positive node is a probability, not a diagnosis. Granulomatous disease, anthracosis, reactive nodes draining a post-obstructive pneumonia and sarcoidosis all take up FDG happily, and in a population with any burden of tuberculosis or histoplasmosis the false positive rate is high enough to matter. The decision hanging on this node is enormous \u2014 single-station N2 disease moves a resectable patient into multimodality treatment \u2014 so guidelines require pathological confirmation of PET-positive mediastinal nodes, usually by endobronchial ultrasound with mediastinoscopy in reserve. Note also that lung cancer is staged by TNM 9th edition, which subdivides N2 by single versus multiple station involvement, making accurate nodal mapping more consequential than it used to be. Waiting three months simply lets a curable cancer grow.",

changes.before: "explain": "Mucinous and signet ring adenocarcinomas have low cellular density and abundant extracellular mucin, so there are simply fewer glycolytic cells per voxel and uptake is modest even in large tumours. The same trap recurs across the false negative list: well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumours, lepidic-predominant lung adenocarcinoma, indolent lymphomas such as marginal zone and MALT, renal cell and hepatocellular carcinoma, and prostate adenocarcinoma. Lesion size compounds it \u2014 below roughly 8 to 10 mm partial volume averaging dilutes true uptake towards background, so two 9 mm liver lesions could not be called benign on PET even in an avid tumour. Liver MRI with a hepatobiliary or diffusion-weighted protocol is the sensitive test here, and rectal MRI still does the local staging that PET cannot.",

changes.before: "explain": "Metformin produces striking, continuous FDG uptake through small bowel and colon, thought to reflect increased enterocyte glucose handling; where the bowel is the question, stopping it for around 48 hours before the scan clears the picture. That diffuse pattern is not itself an indication for colonoscopy. Focal colonic uptake is a different finding entirely and is the incidental most worth chasing: it appears in something like one or two per cent of oncological PET studies, and in pooled colonoscopy series a large minority \u2014 of the order of a third \u2014 prove to be an adenoma or a carcinoma. A polyp found this way is a cure. Report it explicitly and name the segment, because the endoscopist will otherwise not know where to look.",

Focal colonic uptake is a different finding entirely and is the incidental most worth chasing: it appears in something like one or two per cent of oncological PET studies, and in pooled colonoscopy series a large minority — of the order of a third — prove to be an adenoma or a carcinoma. A polyp found this way is a cure. Report it explicitly and name the segment, because the endoscopist will otherwise not know where to look.",

changes.before: "explain": "Focal thyroid incidentalomas appear on around one to two per cent of FDG studies, and pooled series put the malignancy rate at roughly 25 to 35 per cent \u2014 high enough that ignoring it is indefensible, low enough that most are benign. The proportionate response is ultrasound first, then risk-stratify by sonographic features using ACR TI-RADS or the local equivalent, and aspirate on that basis rather than on the PET alone. Diffuse thyroid uptake is a different finding, usually chronic autoimmune thyroiditis, and needs only thyroid function tests if there is a clinical reason. The same graded logic applies to incidental focal prostate uptake: check the PSA and refer for urological assessment rather than either ignoring it or launching straight into biopsy. Always weigh it against the prognosis of the cancer being staged.",

changes.before: "explain": "Under the explicitly supplied two-point mono-exponential model, ADC=ln(800/400)/(1000-100)=7.70\u00d710^-4 mm\u00b2/s, or0.77\u00d710^-3 mm\u00b2/s. These hypothetical calibrated inputs must not be borrowed by an uncalibrated source ADC display.",
changes.after: "explain": "Under the explicitly supplied two-point mono-exponential model, ADC=ln(800/400)/(1000-100)=7.70×10^-4 mm²/s, or0.77×10^-3 mm²/s. The calculation assumes the stated b-values, same source region and comparable calibrated acquisitions. ADC depends on b-values, vendor and processing, and benign and malignant tissues overlap. A value within or outside a proposed threshold range does not independently establish or exclude cancer. Interpret qualitative morphology/diffusion and the complete clinical context. These hypothetical calibrated inputs must not be borrowed by an uncalibrated source ADC display.",

changes.before: "answer": "First, stronger diffusion weighting commonly lowers SNR and can require longer echo time or more acquisition effort; the practical result depends on the scanner and protocol. A calculated high-b image is a producer-derived image, not a separately acquired measurement. Second, diffusion kurtosis can make high-b signal depart from a mono-exponential fit, changing the ADC estimate. PI-RADS v2.1 requires a high-b image set of at least1400 s/mm\u00b2, acquired or calculated, and recommends a maximum b-value no greater than1000 s/mm\u00b2 for ADC calculation. Record actual acquisition/derivation, quality, source ROI and calibration.",
changes.after: "answer": "First, stronger diffusion weighting commonly lowers SNR and can require longer echo time or more acquisition effort; the practical result depends on the scanner and protocol. A calculated high-b image is a producer-derived image, not a separately acquired measurement. Second, diffusion kurtosis can make high-b signal depart from a mono-exponential fit, changing the ADC estimate. PI-RADS v2.1 requires a high-b image set of at least1400 s/mm², acquired or calculated, and recommends a maximum b-value no greater than1000 s/mm² for ADC calculation. Record actual acquisition/derivation, quality, source ROI and calibration.",

changes.before: "explain": "PI-RADS v2.1 accepts acquired or calculated high-b images, with at least1400 s/mm\u00b2 for that image set. It recommends no more than1000 s/mm\u00b2 in the ADC calculation to limit diffusion-kurtosis effects on the mono-exponential model. Stronger gradients and higher diffusion weighting impose signal/echo-time and scan-effort tradeoffs, but image quality depends on the actual system. A synthesized image is not automatically cleaner, a measured high-b acquisition or interchangeable calibrated data. Keep its derivation and the ADC fit separate.",
changes.after: "explain": "PI-RADS v2.1 accepts acquired or calculated high-b images, with at least1400 s/mm² for that image set. changes.before: "explain": "Radium-223 is a calcium mimetic: it deposits at sites of high bone turnover, which in this disease means the osteoblastic reaction around metastases. Its alpha particles have a range of only a few cell diameters, under about 100 micrometres, which is exactly why it delivers high linear energy transfer damage to the tumour microenvironment while relatively sparing marrow \u2014 and equally why it does nothing whatever for soft tissue or nodal disease. The ALSYMPCA trial enrolled men with symptomatic bone-predominant disease and no visceral metastases, excluding bulky lymphadenopathy, and showed improved overall survival of roughly 14.9 against 11.3 months with fewer symptomatic skeletal events. Symptomatic bone disease is the indication, not a contraindication. Since ERA-223 found increased fractures when it was combined with abiraterone and prednisolone, that combination is avoided and bone-protective therapy is given.",

changes.before: "explain": "Gallium-68 or fluorine-18 is used for imaging and lutetium-177, a beta emitter, or actinium-225, an alpha emitter, for treatment, mounted on the same vector molecule. The diagnostic study is effectively a whole-body biopsy of receptor expression, sampling every lesion at once \u2014 something no tissue sample can do, and the reason a single negative biopsy does not settle the question. It answers three things: is the target present, is it present in all the measurable disease, and is it bright enough against a reference organ. After treatment, imaging the small gamma yield of lutetium-177 confirms that the activity went where the diagnostic scan predicted, occasionally shows disease not previously seen, and provides the counts for dosimetry.",
changes.after: "explain": "Gallium-68 or fluorine-18 is used for imaging and lutetium-177, a beta emitter, or actinium-225, an alpha emitter, for treatment, mounted on the same vector molecule. The diagnostic study is effectively a whole-body biopsy of receptor expression, sampling every lesion at once — something no tissue sample can do, and the reason a single negative biopsy does not settle the question. It answers three things: is the target present, is it present in all the measurable disease, and is it bright enough against a reference organ. After treatment, imaging the small gamma yield of lutetium-177 confirms that the activity went where the diagnostic scan predicted, occasionally shows disease not previously seen, and provides the counts for dosimetry.",

changes.before: "explain": "Lutetium-177 conveniently emits low-abundance gamma photons at 113 and 208 keV alongside its therapeutic beta particles, so an ordinary gamma camera can image the treatment itself \u2014 a real advantage over pure beta and alpha emitters, where you administer the dose and hope. The study documents biodistribution and confirms delivery to the targets identified at screening; it occasionally reveals additional lesions; and with serial time points it supports patient-specific dosimetry of kidneys, marrow and salivary glands, which is moving steadily from research towards routine practice. The finding that should give you pause is a photopenic area where a known lesion sits, indicating heterogeneous target expression and a region that will not have been treated.",

changes.before: "explain": "The three-layer T2 appearance of the uterus \u2014 bright endometrium, dark junctional zone, intermediate outer myometrium \u2014 is a feature of the reproductive years. The junctional zone is the inner myometrium, where smooth muscle cells are packed more densely with less extracellular water, and it is hormonally responsive. After the menopause, and on the combined oral contraceptive or a gonadotrophin-releasing hormone agonist, it commonly becomes thin or invisible, and the uterus looks uniformly intermediate. That is normal, not disease and not a technical failure. It does mean you lose your inner reference line, so depth is judged against total myometrial thickness on the sequences with the best tumour-to-muscle contrast. Diffuse adenomyosis is not a plausible reading in a 68-year-old with an atrophic uterus, and assuming deep invasion would overtreat. The lesson generalises: interpret zonal anatomy against the patient's hormonal state.",
changes.after: "explain": "The three-layer T2 appearance of the uterus — bright endometrium, dark junctional zone, intermediate outer myometrium — is a feature of the reproductive years. The junctional zone is the inner myometrium, where smooth muscle cells are packed more densely with less extracellular water, and it is hormonally responsive. After the menopause, and on the combined oral contraceptive or a gonadotrophin-releasing hormone agonist, it commonly becomes thin or invisible, and the uterus looks uniformly intermediate. That is normal, not disease and not a technical failure. It does mean you lose your inner reference line, so depth is judged against total myometrial thickness on the sequences with the best tumour-to-muscle contrast. Diffuse adenomyosis is not a plausible reading in a 68-year-old with an atrophic uterus, and assuming deep invasion would overtreat. The lesson generalises: interpret zonal anatomy against the patient's hormonal state.",

changes.before: "explain": "The most consequential change in FIGO 2018 was the creation of stage IIIC, which lets nodal disease raise the stage independently of the local extent of the tumour. IIIC1 is pelvic nodal disease and IIIC2 is para-aortic nodal disease. Because the finding may come from imaging or from pathology, the stage carries a suffix \u2014 r when assigned on imaging and p when assigned on histology \u2014 so this case is IIIC1r. A small primary confined to the cervix with one positive pelvic node is therefore stage III, which sounds startling until you remember that nodal status is among the strongest prognostic factors in this disease. Practically, it usually moves the patient from surgery to definitive chemoradiation, and it changes the radiotherapy volume. Judge nodes on shape, necrosis, irregular border and diffusion as well as size; PET-CT is often added to check the para-aortic chain before the field is drawn.",
changes.after: "explain": "The most consequential change in FIGO 2018 was the creation of stage IIIC, which lets nodal disease raise the stage independently of the local extent of the tumour. IIIC1 is pelvic nodal disease and IIIC2 is para-aortic nodal disease. Because the finding may come from imaging or from pathology, the stage carries a suffix — r when assigned on imaging and p when assigned on histology — so this case is IIIC1r.
